MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN DEPUTY SPEAKER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I interrupted my remarks on the censure motion presented by the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire), I was wondering who was really responsible for that violation of the rules of the house.
Is it the Deputy Speaker? Is it the Prime Minister? Is it the party in office or all the parties, except ours? Those are so many questions which fill my mind.
What did the Deputy Speaker do or rather did not do on the evening of Friday, March 13, between 8 and 10?
Contrary to what the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) gave the house to understand, the Deputy Speaker never asked, as is done usually, the unanimous consent of the house.
Yesterday you heard the hon. member for Lapointe give clear evidence that the Deputy Speaker did not ask the unanimous consent of the house, not even once. Some hon. members, whom I congratulate, were even honest enough to say that we were entirely right.
Unless such a procedure be legalized. After I am through with these few remarks, I would ask you, Mr. Speaker, to tell me whether an hon. member can seek the assent of the house in such a case without going through the Chair. For instance, could I introduce a motion without first requesting that the Speaker ask whether there is unanimous consent?


Yet, that is what the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) did.
I cannot understand how the Secretary of State for External Affairs can persist in denying obvious facts. Even with the assistance of all the shrewdest lawyers you will never be able to deny patent facts.
There is only one thing to do, Mr. Secretary of State for External Affairs, and that is for you to repent and resolve not to do it again.
Who could have influenced the Deputy Speaker to follow such an irregular procedure? We find that question puzzling and for obvious reasons, because if the Speaker's decision were dictated by a party or a party caucus, it would be high time for serious members, although they may be small in number, to draw the attention of the house to this matter, and that would be really urgent.
I mention those facts to the house because I noticed that each of the irregular steps taken by the Deputy Speaker was dictated by the urgency of the situation. As evidence of that you have the fact that the Secretary of State for External Affairs told us yesterday that a world war may have been prevented.
We feel that instead of getting all excited as the major parties did last Friday, it would have been much better to abide by the standing orders and to take a hard look at the situation. Indeed, that is what other members of the United Nations did.
We are still wondering today whether it was necessary to put aside standing orders just to replace 3,500 British soldiers by 1,500 Canadian troops and whether it was worth while to betray the most noble traditions of the house to ensure that our soldiers would be first to reach Cyprus when other United Nations members have not yet finished the formation of their units.
Was it really necessary to jeopardize the very confidence in the rules of this house in order to make expenditures of $3, $4 or perhaps $5 million when England has ventured $1 million only and the United States $2 million for the purpose of settling, maybe, a little family quarrel?
The Secretary of State for External Affairs mentioned also yesterday, as an excuse, the need to keep one's word. This is indeed the Liberals favourite argument. For the sake of keeping one's word, nuclear arms are accepted; for the sake of keeping one's word, the rules are ignored, our small country with a population of 19 million people at the most is thrown into adventures which countries with 140 million dare not embark upon; for the sake of keeping one's word, everything is jeopardized for war, so that there is nothing left for peaceful endeavours.

The Prime Minister seems to have the idiosyncrasy of always committing this country and then forcing the house to-

maintopic: MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN DEPUTY SPEAKER
speechtext: Order. I should remind the hon. member that he should only speak on the motion before us today and abstain from discoursing on other subjects.

maintopic: MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN DEPUTY SPEAKER
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, but it was simply meant as a reply to the arguments which the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) put forward yesterday.
Those, Mr. Speaker, are the reasons for our objections Friday night, and if standing orders had been observed, we would have been able to submit those facts to hon. members before embarking on expenses which we were unable to meet.
However, the future will tell us who was right. Two days more would certainly not have changed anything as regards the fate of the world, but the principles of this house would have been preserved.
Anyway, according to the latest reports, our soldiers are now over there.
May this be a lesson to the house so that our great statesmen who long for honours, medals and titles may know, once for all, that in peacetime as in wartime, or even in the war for peace: "It is no use running fast, if there is no timely start." Indeed, the surest way is to follow the century old rules of the house.
We hold no grudge against the Deputy Speaker, whom we have in high regard and whom, moreover, we pity for having served as a scapegoat. We are acting in this way to remind the various groups of the house that the rules exist for everybody.
Mr. Speaker, the one who makes the law should submit to the law like everybody else.
When this principle is no longer respected, when this standard is bypassed, when party interests have destroyed this barrier, then there will be anarchy throughout the country.
Once again we do not hold a grudge against anybody, but we shall never allow the law to be scorned to such an extent.

I wonder, in similar circumstances, if Liberal members had gone through exactly what we ourselves suffered last Friday they would be prepared to say oh, oh in the house, because the prerogatives and rights of certain members, in this instance the members of our group, were completely disregarded and brushed aside by the Deputy Speaker.

maintopic: MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN DEPUTY SPEAKER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Friday afternoon, I objected to giving the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) leave to present his resolution with a view to sending troops to Cyprus.
At that time the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) were very well aware of the fact that our group did not accept that haste to bring that resolution before parliament while, 48 hours' before, a regular notice could have been given the house to the effect that such a motion would be introduced.
Now last Friday I had to be absent in the evening to go to Three Rivers. The Secretary of State for External Affairs was aware of that. I wonder what happened during the supper hour, between six and eight o'clock, that the Deputy Speaker, at eight o'clock, decided to let the Prime Minister introduce his resolution, although some members of our group objected to the introduction of that resolution at that time.
That is what the Deputy Speaker said, and I quote from page 911 of Hansard:
The Prime Minister asked leave to present the motion and he is proceeding on that basis.
He is admitting that the Prime Minister had not obtained the unanimous consent of the house. But later on there was a request to put the Chair's ruling to the house, in view of the fact that the Chair had asked for the unanimous consent of the house.
Mr. Speaker, there has been a deplorable violation of the rules of the house.
Of course, the leader of the official opposition admitted during the debate yesterday, that parliamentary procedure had not been quite in order, and he blamed the government and the Prime Minister for introducing this motion with too much haste. I quote here what the Leader of the Opposition said, as recorded on page 1209 of Hansard:
For that reason I think some reference should be made to the motion. After all, as Leader of the Opposition, as the Prime Minister has said on more than one occasion, I am an officer of this house.
All through the years I have been one of those who have strongly stood against the actions of any government which would trample on the rights and privileges of the opposition.
Why did the Leader of the Opposition not stand up, since he admits that he was in the house Friday afternoon and Friday night?
I took that view not only when in opposition but also when we enjoyed an overwhelming majority in the house. My desire has been at all times to preserve inviolate the rights and privileges of minorities in this chamber. If we should allow action to be taken that is contrary to the privileges and rules of parliament, then indeed

Non-confidence in Deputy Speaker it will not be very long before the rights of private members are lost. I preface what I have to say by these general observations.
But once everything is over the Leader of the Opposition finds that rules have been broken in his presence in the house.
And here he speaks of his love for minorities and for our small number of members; he goes on, as reported on the same page of Hansard:
I think the government was responsible for what happened.
The Leader of the Opposition is just as responsible as the government.
Certainly, there was haste.
It is somewhat late to admit it.
Certainly there was a desire on the part of members generally to carry out the responsibility of this nation.
Who are those to whom this nation has expressed the wish that the government introduce with haste a resolution for the shipping of troops overseas or to Cyprus?
When was the Canadian nation consulted? When did the Canadian nation authorize us, ask us to send troops to Cyprus or submit to the government the resolution which the Prime Minister introduced forcibly in the house last Friday evening?
Then the Leader of the Opposition himself goes on to say, as recorded on page 1209 of Hansard, and I quote:
He-
The Leader of the Opposition was then referring to the Prime Minister.
He had no leave. No leave had been asked for and no leave had been given.
That is what the Leader of the Opposition said yesterday afternoon, but Friday he let the rules be violated and trampled down right here in this house.
When I say that, I in no way mean to imply that a refractory few should be able to hold up the operations of this house.
Just imagine. There are today minorities and small groups, and they would have fought to safeguard the rights of a member of the House of Commons duly elected by the voters. And he continues:
-I in no way mean to imply that a refractory few should be able to hold up the operations of this house. However, these are the rules. When the rules were brought into effect, parliament was not bifurcated or trifurcated or divided into a multiplicity of opposition groups.
I want the Leader of the Opposition to know that if a member of his political party in this house had been involved, I would have objected in exactly the same way. The Leader of the Opposition contradicted himself glaringly concerning disrespect for the rules.
[Mr. Caouette.l
And the Leader of the Opposition goes on:
I would be the last to fail to rise to defend the right of one member in this house against unfairness. What took place is past. What we are now being asked to do is to place the stigma of responsibility for wrongdoing on the Deputy Speaker. That stand I will not take.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to state clearly that it is not through antipathy that we introduced a motion against the Deputy Speaker, for I have a great respect for my friend the hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Lamoureux), since he has always been up to now completely unprejudiced, but I am inclined to think that last Friday evening, a member of the government, either a minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) or the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) himself has used his influence on the Deputy Speaker to ask him to allow the resolution to be introduced so that it would be ready at 8.02 p.m. The government is to blame for this.
Mr. Speaker, if it is fully intended to have the standing orders complied with, whether by members of the Liberal party or of other groups in the house, it is up to the Speaker or Deputy Speaker to see to it. Now, we are told two days later that a mistake has been made.
I disagree with the allegations of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who said we had made a mistake, when he did not have the courage to rise in order to plead urgency. This matter seemed so urgent because our troops had to be sent without delay, and that was the reason for introducing this resolution.
Now, it appears that Sweden and Ireland do not have any troops in Cyprus yet, that Canadians are the only ones there, and the Secretary of State for External Affairs is aware of that situation. Then, why such urgency? Was it for restoring peace in Cyprus or was it for the purpose of climbing another step towards a Nobel prize, in the near or the distant future?
Mr. Speaker, we are the first to wish to abide by the rules of the house and we are asking the other members to do the same.
In closing, I want to reassert that we have nothing against the Deputy Speaker, but let it not happen again.
When the government wants to introduce a motion, it should ask for the unanimous consent of the house, and if a member, whatever the party to which he belongs, is against it, the rules should be respected. The rules should be respected, otherwise we will see new disorder similar to what happened last Friday evening.
We do not have a grudge against the Deputy Speaker, but the Liberal members who try to intervene in the debate would be the

first to object if they were sitting in the opposition, they would be the first to condemn that violation of the rules of the house.
Mr. Speaker, we ask that, from now on, the rules be complied with and not only by one group, but by all members of the house.

speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-76, to amend the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1960, with respect to representation of the provinces in the Senate and qualifications of senators.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SENATE REPRESENTATION FROM QUEBEC
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SENATE REPRESENTATION FROM QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill seeks primarily to make the Senate more Canadian, especially concerning the province of Quebec which, until now, was not governed by the same regulations as the other Canadian provinces. As you can see in the explanatory notes, it is proposed mainly to replace section 23 which states that a person must:
be over the age of 30, be a British subject, etc.
by the following:
1.	Be over 30 years of age;
2.	Be a Canadian citizen;
3.	Reside in the province which the senator represents.
I fail to see why the province of Quebec should be treated differently from the other provinces as far as the Senate is concerned.
The purpose of this bill is to give Quebec exactly the same rights and prerogatives as the other Canadian provinces.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the function of the United Nations force in Cyprus, in accordance with the resolution of the security council of March 4, is to use its best efforts to prevent a recurrence of fighting and as necessary to contribute to the restoration and maintenance of law and order and a return to normal conditions. The role of the Canadian contingent, and of the forces contributed by other countries, is to undertake such duties as may be ordered by the commander of the force to carry out this mission.

That is too bad.

Secretary of State for External Affairs has agreed with this stipulation on Canada's behalf?

Yes, Mr. Speaker. This does not mean, however, that the forces will not be allowed, as would be the situation in the case of any police force, to defend themselves.

May I ask a
supplementary question. Have any precise directives yet been given to the Canadian forces in Cyprus by the U.N. command?

The acting commander is in charge of the United Nations international force. The instructions which will be given to the forces will go from him and from the commander, General Gyani, who takes up his responsibilities on the 21st of this month.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the minister whether he does not feel that the denial to the Canadian forces of their right to disarm guerrillas in fact emasculates the Canadian force and places the force in a position of great danger.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not agree with the right hon. gentleman. This was one of the questions which were the subject of considerable discussion prior to the decision of the government to answer the call of the secretary general. It was one of the subjects which I discussed with him a week ago tonight in his office at the United Nations. From all the information available to the secretary general and to others, it seemed in the circumstances that one of the best ways to preserve order was to leave to the government and to the communities concerned these responsibilities at this stage. I believe that if the force can establish peace and order, as thus far it seems to have been able to do, this would be a better arrangement. The secretary general has indicated that from time to time the situation will have to be re-examined in the light of events.

A supplementary question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. As the Secretary of State for External Affairs has indicated that the United Nations commander General Gyani has not yet taken over, under what precise directives are the Canadian forces there now acting?

They are acting, Mr. Speaker, under the instructions being given to them by the secretary general. He has provided, in the guide lines, which have been made public, the following: First of all, he has stated to the security council that the U.N. force in Cyprus is in being; second, that troops of the Canadian contingent have been taken under command of the acting

Inquiries of the Ministry commander, Major General C.F. Paiva Chaves; and third, that the force will be established operationally when sufficient troops are available to it in Cyprus to make it possible for it to discharge its functions effectively.
While I am on my feet, Mr. Speaker, perhaps this would be an opportune moment to give the house a message which was sent to our ambassador by the secretary general of the United Nations, U Thant. He wrote as follows:
My Dear Ambassador,
I would be grateful if you would convey to your government my warm appreciation of its favourable response to my appeal for a contingent for the United Nations peace keeping force in Cyprus. I know that the decision to provide a contingent in the circumstances of the Cyprus problem cannot have been an easy one to take and favourable action is all the more valued for that reason. The fine support of your government at this critical time has been a vital factor in the United Nations ability to meet its responsibility for trying to bring peace to the island of Cyprus. Already the knowledge that your government is making troops available is having a steadying influence on the situation and I am sure that the early arrival of those troops will make a far more positive contribution to the peace effort there. I look forward to close co-operation with you and your government on this question in the coming weeks.
Yours sincerely,
U Thant

Mr. Speaker, the minister referred to the force being operational. I wonder how he would reconcile "operational" with the restrictions which are being placed upon it, as we understand the matter; and would he not agree that it would appear to many of us who have had experience in this field that because of these restrictions the situation of our troops there is made absolutely hopeless?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret the statement of the hon. gentleman. I am sure that on reflection he will share my regret. This is a very difficult situation involving deep tensions and hostilities between two communities, in which there are a number of armed citizens who have been contributing to the tension and bloodshed in the island. The forces that will go in there under the command of General Gyani will be armed. They are, however, not in there as occupational troops. They are there for the purpose of preserving order, and it seems to us that troops that are sent to the island will want to emphasize that they are there primarily for that purpose and not to act in a way that could add to their very difficult assignment. They will be armed and they will have every right to take those precautions in advance which this house properly expects them to take. The situation in the island


continues to be one of calm and this has been contributed to undoubtedly-

speechtext: There was an outbreak yesterday.

Mr. Speaker, this house has learned from long experience that, the more difficult the position in which the minister finds himself, the longer he takes to reply. We take that for granted. I appreciate the problem he has raised. No one questions the difficulty of the situation but I ask him how he defines "self defence"? Can you only defend yourself after you have been killed?

I would say to my hon. friend that you certainly do not define it by using the words my hon. friend used, by saying that the situation confronting the Canadian contingent was a hopeless one. It is not a hopeless one.
Of course not.

It is not hopeless because the United Nations forces are contributing to a situation that is getting better and better. My hon. friend asked a specific question. He knows the answer. speechtext: I have already answered the first part of my hon. friend's question. He may not be satisfied with the answer, but it is the answer which I have given. This matter was the subject of considerable discussion between the secretary general and those who spoke for Canada. At this stage the secretary general does not propose to institutionalize the consultative arrangements, but I may assure my hon. friend that there are good reasons for the position he takes. I did not agree with the position he took last week, but after talking to him I appreciate the reasons and I am satisfied that at the present time they are good reasons. I may assure my hon. friend that Canada will be fully consulted.

It is true that today we were told by the press that some fighting had broken out in one particular area between the two communities. This situation has been going on for some time; but since the announcement by the secretary general that he had established a police force the situation has become calmer. I was told by the ambassador of Cyprus to the United Nations, who visited Ottawa this morning, that it was correct to say that as a result of the establishment of the force, a period of tranquillity had set in, and he hoped and believed that this would continue to be the situation. No one can guarantee this, but I am sure that the Canadians in the United Nations force and the force itself will do everything they humanly can to do what they have been sent there to do in the name of the United Nations, that is, seek to preserve order.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to know if the minister can seriously 20220-79
Inquiries of the Ministry describe as a condition of tranquillity a situation where people are being killed and murdered?

speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, March 16, consideration of the motion of Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to continue the debate which I adjourned the other evening I would say that one has had an opportunity to look over the budget address of my hon. friend in a quieter atmosphere than the rather frenzied aura which always prevails, and properly so, on the occasion of the presentation of the budget. I must say that, having read it over carefully in the past day or two, I sometimes wonder why I did not conclude the debate the other evening instead of going on for any length of time today, because there certainly is not a great deal in the budget presentation of the minister on which one can make any serious, critical comments, or critical commentary, as far as that is concerned.
It is so different from the atmosphere last year. Hon. members will remember the arrival of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) on that occasion, with all the solutions 20220-80
The Budget-Mr. Nowlan to the nation's problems wrapped up in his brief case, and he presented them to us. There was a whole bookful: they were going to rectify foreign ownership of Canadian industry; they were going to do this, they were going to do that, and they were going to do the other thing. For various reasons that budget, as I said the other night, has been improved upon from time to time because most of the provisions in it have since been dropped. Instead of having, shall I say, a superman arriving to present the budget as we had a year ago, this time we had Mickey Mouse coming in with a very, very small parcel.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This makes the position of an opposition critic, the financial critic or anyone else, rather difficult. I have a quote here which I should like to read to the house. I am not going to quote from newspapers this afternoon to any extent, Mr. Speaker, because I do not intend to speak at any great length; but I have one newspaper quotation which is apropos of what I have said, and which I came across only this afternoon. I am sure it will commend itself to the minister, because it is in keeping with the thought I just expressed. This editorial was in the Quebec Chronicle-Telegraph of March 18 and it says:
After a year of almost continuous labour, the mountain, apparently, has brought forth a mouse- It is a poor, timorous thing wrapped up in large swaddling clothes.
I do not think any better comment than that can be made on the budget. As I said, Mr. Speaker, I am not going into this matter at great length this afternoon. I do not think I can finish before five o'clock, but I shall not go very much beyond that. There are certain things, of course, in the budget of which we entirely approve. As I said the other night when I was asked about this on the radio, and the question was whether there was anything in the budget of which we approved, "I have not brought my microscope with me and could not answer that question at this time". But having produced my microscope in the meantime, I can say there are some things of which we do approve. We approve, of course, of the provisions with regard to educational advantages. We approve of the deduction of tuition fees for part-time students; the deduction by either a brother or sister for-if I may introduce a new term here-a sibling dependant attending school. We also endorse the proposed extension of family allowances and commend the minister and his associates for their remarkably quick conversion in this regard because, having voted against this most important provision

The Budget-Mr. Nowlan only a few weeks ago, they embraced it to their bosoms and brought it forward in the person of Her Majesty's Minister of Finance. This was really a remarkable conversion and one for which I would commend the Minister of Finance. I have used this simile before, but the conversion of Saul of Tarsus on his way to Damascus was not as rapid as that of the minister and his associates in this connection.
We entirely approve, of course, of the incentives contained in the budget which, as the minister said, are directed toward certain areas in need of economic expansion. As I recall it, the minister referred particularly to certain areas in Quebec and also to the Atlantic provinces. I am glad to see that the minister is extending the period of these incentives so they will be longer in operation. I am not sure, Mr. Speaker, just what the reason may be. It may be that the incentives have proven so useful that the minister feels they should be extended; or perhaps so far they have not been taken advantage of at all, or very, very little, and the minister thought that by extending the period for a year or two more he might be able to get some people to take advantage of them. I realize that these incentives are difficult to administer. I also doubt, frankly, the efficacy of some of the incentives which the minister projected.
It is not his fault that they are not effective, but I doubt very much the efficacy of them. I would suggest to the minister that in the province with which I am more acquainted than any other, namely the province of Nova Scotia, he will find the incentives and leadership given by the government of that province, through Industrial Estates Limited, in the development of industry have been far greater than that which has flowed from any of the incentives which he has put forward thus far. When we hear, as we undoubtedly will, from the Minister of Finance, who is, of course, a very modest individual, or perhaps from the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury), as to the developments which have taken place in the province of Nova Scotia, I hope that they will-and if they do not, some of us on this side of the house will have to-distinguish between what may have flowed, if anything, from the incentives to which the Minister of Finance has referred, and to which he referred again the other night, and the work done in the province of Nova Scotia which has given a tremendous impetus to and leadership in the industrial development of that province.
In that connection I should like to make reference to the only newspaper report to which I will draw the attention of the minister this afternoon dealing with the matter of

incentives. It is an editorial which appeared in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald for March 17 last, in which is discussed the question of incentives as particularly applying to the maritime provinces. This editorial says, in part, that the minister could, and should, have done more to encourage economic growth through further tax incentives. It points out what the paper looks upon-and I concur with this paper in this regard, although I do not always-as limiting incentives to specific areas, and suggests that there should be a more all-embracing area covering the province as a whole, rather than picking out one town in one county and another area in another county. That is not the way.
I cannot speak with authority obviously on a large province such as Ontario, with which the minister is thoroughly conversant, but in a smaller province like Nova Scotia you cannot pick out one town in one county, and another town in another county, and have the incentives apply as they should. The Halifax Chronicle-Herald recommends that these incentives be broadened so as to cover larger areas, and I think that is a suggestion which is well worth following. These are some of the matters, Mr. Speaker, of which one can speak with commendation to the minister for having brought them forward.
And may I say, Mr. Deputy Speaker, that we are glad to see you in the chair.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron) referred to the budget the other night as small potatoes and few in the hill, a very pastoral expression which I think he must have picked up in the maritime provinces because I heard it used by my grandfather who lived in Digby county many years ago. But I should like to use a more apt description of the budget than the one to which he has referred and say that it is more like a timorous mouse.
I should like to discuss for a few moments, although I will not be able to finish my remarks on this point before five o'clock, one change which the minister has made and which has aroused a great deal of comment by the financial press during the last few days. I am referring to the changes which he has made in the withholding tax. You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that the minister proposed last year a withholding tax which we on this side of the house criticized very strongly. We said that it was discriminatory; we said that it could not be applied; we said that it would invite retaliation and that it would be necessary to negotiate a new tax convention between Canada and the United States if it was to be effective; and we said that time would not permit such a negotiation to take place.

The minister questioned these criticisms of ours and then went ahead with his program, although he altered and amended it in various ways during the next two, three or tour successive budgets which he brought down. But he still maintained the difference between the 20 per cent and the 10 per cent. It one did not accept a certain amount ot Canadian participation one would be required to pay a withholding tax of 20 per cent. On the other hand, if one did one would only pay a withholding tax of 10 per cent. He made a differentiation, as I told the minister last year, as between the good boys and the bad boys, and on that aspect alone we did not think that this proposal of the minister was a sound principle to bring into tax legislation.
This year the minister tells us that he was in Washington a short time ago, that he had found a new element had entered the situation, and consequently that he was going to amend the tax. The new element was that the United States senate had brought in a bill to reduce taxation, and for some reason which I am not going to try to follow for the moment-quite frankly, I cannot follow the minister anyway on this-he said that because of this new factor he was now prepared to amend his proposals; and perhaps I may be permitted to suggest how this should be done after we resume the debate at eight o'clock. However, I should like to point out to the minister at this stage that this new factor of the reduction of the tax-the proposal before the United States senate to reduce taxation-was before the United States senate last year, as I recall it, before the minister amended this provision for the second or the third time. So therefore it could not have been a new factor, because it was already before the United States senate. I think it was recognized by the United States press that this tax reduction bill would go through, so the minister cannot be heard to say today that this was a new factor in the situation.
However, I do suggest that the new factor is this. When the minister was in Washington a few weeks ago secretary Dillon told him that his proposal was bound to invite retaliation; that the increase to 20 per cent, of course, would require a new tax convention; and that it was impossible to renegotiate such a convention before December 31, 1964.
Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that a student in grade nine political science would know that this year, with the heavy legislative burden which is before the United States senate-without going into the details of it- with the protracted debates which have already taken place and which will, according to every newspaper report I have read, continue for a long while to come, and with an 20220-80i
Motions for Papers
election in the offing and one third of the senate to be re-elected, and with naturally the other two thirds supporting their colleagues taking part in the election either in the senate or the house of representatives, there would be very little hope for any renegotiation of a tax treaty. As we pointed out, if this was not done there would be an automatic 30 per cent withholding tax as at December 31 this year. Therefore this was not a new factor but was a gradual recognition on the part of the minister that the things which we on this side of the house said were true and correct, and he had to reconcile himself to them in his budget.
May I call it five o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

The house resumed from Thursday, March 12, consideration of the following motion of Mr. Bell:

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Kellyer (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week in the two or three minutes available to me I had outlined some of the background in relation to the situation in which we found ourselves in connection with the security of national defence property in general, and small arms and ammunition in particular. As I indicated, there had been some concern throughout a number of months with respect to the security of small arms, and steps had been taken to tighten up the security precautions in respect thereto.
Following the raid on the armoury in Montreal on January 30 this process was accelerated in order to remove the temptation to attempt another such incident from anyone who might be inclined to do so. As I indicated, on January 31, the very day following the raid, immediate action was taken. A commission was set up and that commission was asked to study the security regulations in respect of national defence property, and to make recommendations as to any steps which should be taken to improve the security measures.
Simultaneously some of the services issued orders to tighten up the observation of

Motions for Papers
existing regulations in respect ol security. Interim measures were taken which required that rifles be stored separately from their working parts, separately from the bolts and from the ammunition. Consequently, as I indicated, from that day forward no useable arms were taken.
When the commission reported, it recommended the immediate withdrawal of small arms until adequate security precautions could be put into effect. This was ordered at once for sensitive areas. As I indicated, it was carried out with zeal and there have been no losses since that time. Simultaneously across the country security measures already in existence were being enforced more rigidly than had been the case, and in a number of cases arms and ammunition were removed temporarily until such time as the regulations could be met. Arms and ammunition removed from various installations were placed in installations where they could be given round the clock security, and even in those installations where arms were no longer in inventory additional watchmen were required to provide more general surveillance of national defence property.
The suggestion has been made that round the clock guards should be put on all national defence installations, including reserve units. I really think that on reflection hon. members will appreciate that this is not a practicable suggestion. In this country we have had no history of providing round the clock armed security for our reserve units, with some exceptions, those exceptions being at times like the Fenian raids and when there was some indication of riot or insurrection. With those exceptions there never has been any attempt to provide uniform, round the clock security for our reserve installations.
The magnitude of the problem is really very great. If anyone felt that such a course should be followed, I think he would have to look very carefully at the manpower required and the cost in dollars which would be involved. To provide really adequate round the clock security for all our reserve units would require the employment of thousands of men and the cost would run into many millions of dollars a year. In my opinion this is not a practicable solution. In this regard another recommendation was made by the commission set up in the Department of National Defence and which, as I have indicated earlier, included a representative of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Their recommendation was that other measures be taken which would provide adequate security, make it very difficult to effect the removal of small arms and ammunition and not require round the clock armed guards.
[Mr. Hellyer.l
These measures are being studied and will be implemented just as quickly as possible.
Many of the arms that have been withdrawn have already been reinstated in areas where this could be done under adequate security measures. This process will continue just as expeditiously as it is possible to do a proper job of inspection, and just as soon as the requirements can be adequately met.
I think the important point is that the action which was taken, as the result of a situation which we all regretted and deplored, has been effective. It has been commented upon favourably by a number of newspapers in their editorial columns, and we are grateful for their support. There have been one or two misapprehensions. For example, the Montreal Gazette in an editorial on February 25, I believe-I am not sure that was the date it appeared-fully supported the program of withdrawing serviceable firearms and ammunition from armouries and other reserve army establishments where security cannot be provided on a round the clock basis. The editorial went on to say:
This is the necessary move. It is imperative that it be taken now. It would have been preferable had it been taken earlier.
The editorial goes on to say:
But there is one aspect of the defence minister's statement that is uncertain. Mr. Hellyer says that orders have gone out that at least one person is to be on duty at reserve establishments at all hours of the day or night. Does this mean that firearms and ammunition will still be left in reserve establishments, provided that they have one armed guard?
The answer is no. I do not think there was any lack of clarity in the statement. The statement was that during this period at least arms and ammunition would only be stored where adequate round the clock protection was available; and the one person on duty at all hours referred to the defence establishments where there were no arms or ammunition but where other national defence properties were in inventory. I might also say that we received co-operation from people across the country, and I should like to pay tribute to them for their co-operation, which is very much appreciated. I have one letter I should like to read, with the indulgence of the house, which I think is indicative of the spirit of co-operation. It is addressed to me and reads as follows:
Honourable Sir:
It is with disgust that I read almost daily of the sentiment of various M.P.'s as well as editors of newspapers across the country re the picking up of arms from the various cadet corps across the country.
As the chief instructor of one of the largest, if not the largest, cadet corps in eastern Ontario, namely, the No. 2403 St. Lawrence high school cadet corps, I must state that the person concerned at Ashbury College in Ottawa who is continually

complaining about the pick-up of arms from that college knew, and I am sure of this, that they would pick up the said arms and he was notified well in advance of same. I know this because I was notified at 7 p.m. and the rifles were picked up here between 12 midnight and 1.30 a.m. on the same day, and I didn't kick as it was my duty to be prepared.
So far all it is worth you can mention my name in the house and I will vouch for same. I am sure that all concerned were notified but there are some who fail to comply with an order even though they are members of Her Majesty's forces and have taken the oaths of office.
I commend, and I wish you would mention this in the house, the eastern Ontario area cadet training officer for the method in which he instructed his men to take out arms.
The majority of papers in eastern Ontario and also in Toronto have published news about matters they knew nothing about whatsoever and I deem it their fault that this has come to such a ridiculous stage.
I would also like mentioned in the house, if you see fit, that St. Lawrence high school has the crack cadet rifle team in Canada, and not Windsor. We have had various trophies come to Canada in the past few years from England, such as the Young Rifleman's trophy which had never been won before by a Canadian and this being won by the cadet who came first in Ontario and third in Canada in the Dominion of Canada Rifle Association at Connaught ranges.
I am pleased with my corps. I am pleased with the wonderful co-operation we have received from army headquarters. I am sure our hon. member L. Lamoureux can vouch for this.
I trust this has enlightened you some in your big job at present and if I can be of any further assistance to you in this important matter be free to call on me.
(Major) C. H. Paulin

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Is he an officer in the cadet corps?

He is the chief instructor. I think this is typical of the general attitude of co-operation which we have had across the country. May I again say how much we appreciate the indulgence of all concerned. Most people have, I think, recognized that the situation was difficult and that some unusual action was required in the face of the circumstances. They have been understanding and sympathetic in their reaction.
I do not believe I will take more time of the house, but may I reiterate that the armed forces have carried out with dispatch their assigned task of tightening up security in respect of small arms and ammunition, because they have them as a trust and it is their responsibility to make sure that they cannot be easily removed from national defence installations and fall into unauthorized hands. These tasks have been carried out very well so far. We have been completely successful in what we have done. I am sure we will have the support and co-operation of all members of the house in respect of this very difficult situation. I can also assure hon. members that just as quickly as the situation can be restored so that normal
Motions for Papers
training can be resumed in all parts of the country, this will be done. It will be done under circumstances which will limit, just as much as we possibly can with reasonable cost, the possibility of arms and ammunition falling into unauthorized hands in the future.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister did not say anything about the motion that is before us, which is for an order of the house for a copy of all letters, memoranda or directives made by the minister and/or the Department of National Defence regarding the rounding up of arms and/or ammunition. This is what is before us. The minister has simply put up a defence, in his opinion, of the action that was taken. The course of the debate has not been restricted entirely to the production of these particular documents. Certainly, in the light of the minister's reply, since he did not deal with the motion at all, I presume the debate is wide open.
The reasons for asking for this type of information were set out very clearly by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) on March 12 as recorded at page 841 of Hansard. It is rather unusual to request the production of documents which, you may say, are interdepartmental documents. However, as the hon. member for Saint John-Albert pointed out, the circumstances are unusual. Reference has been made quite often by the minister to the fact that directives were not carried out in the same way in all areas. Naturally one wonders, therefore, if it would not be in the public interest to disclose the directive that he sent out, and then we would be clear. The letter which he has just finished reading to us mentioned the fact that orders were received. Were those the orders that came direct from the minister, or to what orders or directives is the writer referring?
Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, I thought it was a most unusual and inappropriate action for the minister to read a letter from a cadet instructor, a letter addressed to the Minister of National Defence. In the first instance, I should like to know why a cadet instructor would write directly to the Minister of National Defence. There is a chain of command to be followed in the services. Apparently, the minister permits cadet instructors to write to him, and now encourages them by this public action. Does he get letters directly from other cadet corps instructors and from his navy, army and air force personnel in the junior ranks? It is a very strange thing indeed. I think the minister is seriously at fault in setting up one cadet instructor against another. Here you have one cadet instructor saying, in effect, pay no attention to the complaints from your people at Ashbury College

Motions for Papers
because everything went all right in our area; pay no attention to the complaints of other cadet corps instructors.
The Minister of National Defence, with responsibility for hundreds of cadet corps across this country, should not be publicly playing one off against the other. I think the minister had better re-examine the responsibilities of his position or we will have a rather odd situation in this country in which people ignore the normal means of communication within the services and are communicating directly with the minister. Then, you begin to wonder, for what purpose? If the minister is going to commend in this way one cadet instructor, why not commend them all or tell us the ones of which he does not approve? Why does he raise this particular issue here in the House of Commons? It is an absolutely inappropriate action.
There would be no motion on the order paper if the minister had been more forthcoming in the answers he gave to a whole host of questions that have been asked in the last several weeks. This trouble began with a raid on the armoury in Montreal which occurred almost 80 days ago; we are into the twelfth week now since this occurred and we have had no satisfactory answers from the minister concerning that particular event. There was another robbery at Shawinigan Falls and attempts elsewhere, and then we had this haphazard action in connection with the cadet corps. Had the minister given information to the house clearly and without evasion, we would not have this motion before us at the moment. He has not been clear and he has certainly been evasive.
Even in reply to a simple written question I put on the order paper, asking him to indicate the areas in which arms and ammunition had been taken from the cadet corps, he stated that it was not in the public interest to give this information. Yet we were reading in the press about one cadet corps after another where some incident had taken place, and he did not tell us to what cadet corps the weapons had been returned.
All of this had made the minister look a bit foolish, and we would like to find out whether or not he was clear in the instructions he gave to the people under his command. I think he must have been very confused himself.
I started this whole train of thought on Wednesday, February 19, as recorded at page 9 of Hansard for that date, when I asked him a question about the thefts, and in answer to that he said:
I also directed that appropriate action be taken to increase security measures at all military establishments at which weapons and ammunition were stored.

Then he went on to say:
Ammunition was removed and put in storage at protected depots.
That was his appropriate action. He did not give the date, but it followed some time after the theft from the Montreal armoury, and subsequently he apparently appointed a commission. This is what he does whenever a problem comes up; he appoints a commission or sets up a special committee. He has untold numbers of officers in the services who can be assembled at a moment's notice, without necessarily making them into committees or commissions, in order to get advice and immediately give instructions.
Surely this problem could have been handled by the chiefs of staff on the very day it came to their attention that there was some difficulty concerning protection for arms and ammunition in the armouries? But the minister said it was a very large problem and it had to be investigated very carefully. He had to find out how many armouries there were and where they were located, how many cadet corps there were and where they were located, but yet right across the country there were area commands where this information could have been available at a moment's notice. By one call on the telephone he could have had a report from every one of those areas; but no, he appointed a commission to look into it and then waited for its recommendations.
He also told us that after he took immediate action, that is, after January 30, no useable arms were subsequently removed. Is he prepared to say that the arms taken at Shawinigan Falls on February 20 were not useable? Rifles and pistols were removed from that armoury on February 20 and they have not yet been recovered.
Further, the minister talked about the impossibility of providing around the clock protection for reserve units. That is understandable, depending where the reserve units are, but it is not understandable with regard to the armouries which are not so great in number that they could not be protected. In some small towns, and areas where militia units have rented quarters, one could not expect around the clock protection, but surely the armouries, which are not that numerous, could have been provided with around the clock protection, and then there would be nothing for us to worry about?
The minister has done something else which has bothered me very seriously. When questions have been asked in this house he has shifted the responsibility. He did this only last Thursday, as recorded at page 846 of Hansard for that day, when he said:
Immediately the commission reported, action was taken the very next day to implement the recommendations made for immediate action.

Then he drew attention to the fact that:
-local commanders have been made responsible for the security of the weapons in their command, and for the carrying out of orders. It has been on their responsibility that a number of weapons have been removed and precautionary measures taken.
Surely it is on the responsibility of the minister. I interjected and said:
You are blaming it on the services.
He replied that he was not. I can give other instances where he shifted the responsibility and put the blame on the services. He certainly did not come to the protection of his serving officers when complaints were made in this house about these actions.
Just have a look sir, at page 457 of Hansard for March 3 last, where the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) is recorded as asking the following supplementary question:
I want to ask the minister if these different interpretations are due to lack of clarity in the minister's order, or to incompetence on the part of the commanders, or to a desire on their part to embarrass the minister because he has been taking away some of their toy soldiers?
The minister had nothing to say. He did not answer that question, and I only wish the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam were present in this chamber when I am speaking of him. I did not like that question. I thought the minister should have immediately accepted the full responsibility and said it was due to lack of clarity in his order. He should have denied that there was incompetence on the part of the commanders.
An accusation now stands on the records of this house that the members of the services are incompetent, and the Minister of National Defence had nothing to say in their defence. Surely he might have denied that if they took inappropriate actions it was not, in the words of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, due to "a desire on their part to embarrass the minister"?
Does he agree that these inappropriate actions, as he has indicated they were, were taken to embarrass him, and why did he not say something about the last phrase used by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam-"because he has been taking away some of their toy soldiers"? There was not a word from the minister. That was just another one of those snide remarks against people in the services, against people in the militia, against cadet instructors and cadet corps. Who are these toy soldiers? I do not mind if people who have smelled gunpowder talk about toy soldiers, but why are we subjected to remarks like this by people in public life, without any defence on the part of the minister?
Motions for Papers

On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I did not think at that time that the question was worthy of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, and I do not think it is worthy of the hon. gentleman to repeat it now, or rather the allegations contained in it.
That is no question of privilege. That is a statement.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am not repeating it as a question. I am merely indicating that it is the type of question which the minister permitted to go unanswered, and I say the Minister of National Defence should at least stand up for the people in the armed services. They are not privileged to state their position here in the House of Commons. Is there to be acceptance in this country that they are playing at being toy soldiers? Remarks of that type were heard in the 'thirties. Those of us who were in the militia then can remember them, before the outbreak of the second world war. They were made in some areas by people who, perhaps, did not see the service of their country in the way others did.
For the Minister of National Defence to let a remark like that go by without comment was, it seemed to me, indicative of a somewhat discourteous attitude to the people under his command. If they were able to be present here they would reply in no uncertain terms. There is no question about toy soldiering going on now in Cyprus. People in cadet corps, people in the militia, are not playing at being soldiers; they are giving service to their country.
Why does not the minister tell us exactly what directions he gave to the officers under his command, to the militia units in this country and to the cadet corps? Why does he not make the position clear instead of coming to the house and reading some commendatory letter he has received from a friend? Had the minister been seized of the importance of this whole operation he would, surely, have done so. Instead, he has dealt with it flippantly, just as he has dealt with inquiries about the notorious, mysterious, undisclosed and, perhaps, never to be produced white paper.
Why has the hon. gentleman been so flippant about this subject? Why can he not give the House of Commons an indication of the directives he issued with regard to the security of arms and ammunition in this country? He still does not treat the matter with the seriousness it deserves. Sufficient arms and ammunition have been stolen to arm 140 men, and there are 4,000 rounds of ammunition to go with those arms. I am not talking about .22 ammunition which can be

Motions for Papers
bought anywhere; I am talking about this heavier ammunition. This is a serious situation. Adequate protection should be afforded to the storage of arms and ammunition across this country; but this can be done in an effective way, with some coolness, instead of building the operation up into what seems to be a mock display of military efficiency and holding up to ridicule the armed services of this country.
The minister must accept full responsibility for this. It is not part of the hon. gentleman's duty in this house to put the blame on his officials, and those who serve in the armed forces are officials acting under the authority of the Minister of National Defence.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but his time has expired.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Well, I have concluded my remarks. I have intimated that the minister is quite irresponsible in his actions.

I would just like to say, on a question of privilege, again, that as the responsible head of the department I accept full responsibility for the action taken by the department. That is the way our system works and I have never shirked my responsibility, nor will I, nor will I attempt to back away from it in any way.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I am sure, Mr. Speaker, you do not recognize that as a question of privilege. It is just a matter of debate. But if it is a question of privilege I would like the right of reply.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I appreciate the comments of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill). There is obviously no question of privilege here.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this order for return, I should like to refer to what has happened in this house during the last two sessions when one member of the opposition after the other introduced such motions, knowing full well that it was unadvisable or impossible to give them the information they sought.
I wonder where we are going and what the intention is, here in this house, if we continue along that line, since we know very well that a minister is not always in a position to table certain papers.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that in this case the Minister of National Defence should protect the general interests of the country, but on the other hand, he keeps as confidential all information liable to benefit his opponents or

those now involved I think he cannot invoke the prerogative, namely not to give all the information, in order not to give any information at all. Some information could have been given to the house and it would have probably satisfied most of us.
Once more, I realize that the opposition, when introducing this motion for the production of papers, was rather aiming at partisan advantage by stirring prejudices, as they have been doing for some time now. But this is an extremely dangerous demagogy, since this concerns the theft of arms and ammunition which may be used to start a revolution or a coup d'etat.
On the other hand, if such a situation exists in the province of Quebec and if arm robberies took place, we must remember that we share the responsibility, because we helped to arouse feelings which the present government keeps stirring up. It is precisely by practising demagogy in everything related to defence that we share the responsibilities. Newspapers also have their responsibilities, because they gave too much publicity by their headlines to this problem which now faces Quebec and Canada.
The Minister of National Defence is blamed for neglecting to take appropriate steps. If I refer to the early stages of that issue, I remember very well that the opposition at that time made a big fuss, directed questions to the minister to know what he was doing, what he intended to do and why he had done nothing.
Well, today, the opposition complains that the minister committed himself too quickly and that the army acted too hastily. By inference, we come to the conclusion that we have, in this country, three types of government with decreasing power, that is: the army, which seems to be the strongest government in the country, then the civil service, and then the cabinet elected by the people. I wonder if, in carrying out the orders given by the minister, the military authorities did not take priority over the elected authority, that of the cabinet. We can see how a minister can easily be discredited in the public opinion by his own officials and officers.
I think that, in all those succeeding actions, a certain boycott by the army can be detected of the policy worked out by the minister and on which the militia is not necessarily in agreement. The army would like to have a larger share of public funds while the minister, according to decisions taken since he is a member of the cabinet, must cancel certain projects. That new policy was bound to stir up reactions in the army which carried out the orders received with

alacrity and caused certain small difficulties like the one concerning arms stored in armouries.
That being said, I think it is up to the government to act on the problem facing us today.
In my opinion, the minister acted in good faith and knowingly-which is not the case for the opposition. I am quite sure that had the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) been the minister of national defence, he would probably have acted the same way, in such a situation, and not much faster, for the Conservative party has not been known for quick decisions.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I deny that.

Mr. Speaker, if I rise today to take part in this debate, it is to state that I do not share at all the opinion expressed by the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Lessard), who belongs to a party the members of which are slaves to the government.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that what we ask in entirely logical-
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege.
-and that we are entitled to have these documents produced.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency is rising on a question of privilege.
I ask the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm to withdraw the words he said, because I am nobody's slave, least of all, the hon. member's.
Mr. Speaker, to go on with my remarks, I think that the motion submitted by the hon. member-

Mr. Speaker, I would appreciate a ruling from Your Honour on my question of privilege. I think that the words used by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm do not apply and that he should withdraw them.
Mr. Speaker, I named nobody in particular. If the hat fits the hon. member, let him claim it.

Mr. Speaker, that is precisely the reason for which I object to the hon. member's remarks; the hat does not fit me.
Moreover, when he mentioned members of the group of the hon. member for Lake St. John, he attacked me personally. The hat does not fit, and I would ask the hon. member to take it off my head to put it on his own.
Motions for Papers

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps, the remarks of the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm exceeded what he had in mind, and he might explain.

Mr. Speaker, in respect of the question of privilege, I might perhaps modify my remarks and say that the government is the slave of the group of which the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Lessard) is a member. I think that would meet your request.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is altogether logical and in the public interest to ask for the production of these documents, of this correspondence as regards the instructions given by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer).
In fact, I do not think that our request would endanger in any way the security of the state. I know that the Minister of National Defence received instructions from the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) to take such action, and I challenge the minister to put forward a sound and logical reason for not producing those documents.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the minister is not honest in this. He does not want to accede to the official opposition's request because the production of those documents would condemn him and, hence, the Prime Minister of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, we are prepared to co-operate with the government, but it is not through arrogance and in behaving the way they did since the beginning of this session and throughout the last session that they will obtain the collaboration of the loyal opposition. We are doing our duty. We are working in the public interest, and the Minister of National Defence should be the first one to collaborate with all members, in order to clear the situation for the general public on the event that took place.
If the Minister of National Defence and the Prime Minister are responsible for the present disorder and the lack of security in the various armouries, they should take their responsibilities and tell the house the truth, so that the Canadian people may know, once and for all, what to make of all this.

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Cardin (Associate Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to take part in this debate for several reasons.
First, I feel that, from the time those incidents began, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) has given the house just about all the information he was in a position to give and the people had the right to expect. Furthermore, all in all, I think this whole thing is but a tempest in a very cold cup of tea.

Motions for Papers
For some time members ol the opposition have acted as if those incidents were an extremely important matter. And yet, such is not the case.
The circumstances in which the incidents took place may have been unusual, and I realize it must seem strange to many hon. members to find that, for the first time in the history of Canada, our armouries have to be protected.
I think that as soon as it was possible to do so, and immediately after the first theft, the Minister of National Defence and the army authorities took the necessary steps to that end. Since then, the Minister of National Defence has also indicated in the house that there were two kinds of steps that had to be taken.
The first was an emergency measure: weapons scattered throughout the country in armouries and cadet camps had to be stored in safe places; complete security was necessary. People forget that even cadets have not only .22 but also .303 and automatic ones. No risk could be taken and we decided to store them in safe places.
The second step-the minister also pointed it out-was to put these weapons in a place which could be temporarily watched on a round the clock basis. During that period, we had to determine measures which could be carried out in our armouries and our militia establishments in order to assure a greater protection. When that second phase was completed, the arms would then be returned where they came from.
Mention was made of raids. That term was used by members of the opposition, and if the armed forces were held up to ridicule, I think it is due to the opposition.
During all the operations held throughout the country, there were perhaps one or two incidents difficult to explain; but I do not believe anyone is to blame, and certain opinions may not have been entirely well-founded.
It is unfortunate, that attempts were made to play politics with such a small matter.
As for the motion now before us, I believe that if we had to table all the orders and regulations that the Minister of National Defence and myself-and may I say that I accept also the responsibility for what happened-I do not know what would happen. It is possible that the national security may not be in danger, as suggested by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon). But, even then, what purpose would that serve? We would establish a precedent and later on, the minister of defence would be required to table orders and instructions-
Would the minister allow me to ask a question? Does he consider the Department of National Defence as as crown corporation under the present administration?

I do not see the gist of the hon. member's question.
The Department of National Defence must necessarily decide what can be dangerous or what can affect the security of our country or the work we are trying to do. In this case, if we had revealed all the places from which weapons were to be removed, I feel we would have played right into the hands of those who seem to want to steal those weapons.
For those reasons, Mr. Speaker, I claim we are right in refusing to table the orders and directives referred to in this motion.
I might add that there has been no dishonesty here, either on the part of the Minister of National Defence or on mine.
I feel that this should not incite any one in this house to make inaccurate reports which, after all, can only discredit the government and the ministers.
There is also another point which I would like to explain to the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Lessard), who seems to believe that efforts were made among members of the armed forces to embarrass the Minister of National Defence.
Mr. Speaker, may I say to my hon. friend from Lake St. John that there was no such action. On the contrary, we received full co-operation on the part of all superior officers of the Department of National Defence as well as on the part of those who were in charge of those operations. I must say also that we had no doubt about the sincerity of the people in charge of the arms at those places where we took them to put them in a safe place, but that we were afraid, and rightly so, that the arms they had might not be in a safe place and might be stolen, as it had happened, which would have increased the existing danger.
So, Mr. Speaker, I am of the opinion that the Minister of National Defence is quite justified to turn down the motion for papers proposed by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell).

Mr. Speaker, with your permission, I should like to direct only one question to the minister. Would he tell the house whether the orders given by the Department of National Defence concerning armouries and ammunition depots in some parts of the country have been issued in the ten provinces of Canada or only in certain given areas of the country?

Mr. Speaker, we want to provide a little more security for our armouries, and that has been done throughout the country. All we want is to reach a level of security which will avoid the necessity of having a round the clock watch.

Mr. Speaker, the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cardin) has just said that this matter is a tempest in a teapot. He even went so far as to say the teapot was cold. I should like to suggest to him that if he were to come into my part of the country he would soon find that the teapot was not cold, but was quite hot.
In my area of Ontario, and in Wellington South in particular, this is a very important issue. The minister spoke of unusual action being taken. I would say that most unusual action in this regard has been taken in the house in the minister's failure to reveal the directions he issued, and other information asked for by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell). It was also unusual action to issue the instructions he did throughout the country. For instance, in my riding the sea cadet corps were issued with instructions to box up their rifles and ammunition and send them to Quebec, the very province where all this trouble started. You can imagine, Mr. Speaker, what the people in my area thought of that. Why did the minister not order the sea cadet corps to place their guns and ammunition in the armouries in the city of Guelph? Those armouries were built years ago and have walls three feet thick with bars on the windows. There is an iron fence around the building. A three eight-hour shift guard could have been put around the armouries. Lots of soldiers are available, as well as reserves, to do this job of patrolling the armouries, and these guns and ammunition would have been a good deal safer there than in the province of Quebec.
I also think this is unusual action to take in the other provinces throughout Canada, aside from Ontario. Orders have been issued and guns and ammunition have been sent away. In this case we know they went to Quebec, but in many cases we do not know whether they are placed in armouries or somewhere else. We asked the minister to disclose these directives but he has not done so. While these guns and ammunition are away, the reserve forces can no longer train. They are marking time and waiting for their guns and ammunition to be returned.
The minister has talked about unusual action, Mr. Speaker, but I have never seen anything so unusual as this directive which
The Budget-Mr. Nowlan was issued by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) in this particular instance. There are throughout the country armouries which are fortresses, but the minister orders these weapons to be removed from within their walls to some place else.
It is now six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, so I move the adjournment of this debate.
