subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the house began to deal with private members' business at five o'clock I had been discussing the effect of the proposed changes in the withholding tax which the minister brought forward in the budget speech the other night. I was suggesting that the new factor to which he referred was one which was not so new, but was one which we of the opposition had impressed upon him on various occasions during the last year. I do not want to continue to discuss that at this time except to say one further word. The minister, in addition to changing the rate, and bringing it down to 15 per cent, thereby avoiding any break in the ceiling as set forth in the tax convention, also made the spread 15 per cent and 10 per cent. In other words, there is a spread now of only 5 per cent between the good boys and the bad boys. Heretofore it was 20 and 10 and now it is 15 and 10. There will only be that margin of 5 per cent in the withholding tax having regard to whether it is a Canadian corporation, if I may use that term for lack of a better one, or one under foreign control.
Without being unkind, Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that the minister must have decided that these inducements were not too effective and therefore he has now reduced the spread to only 5 per cent. I know the minister and I know he is an optimist, and obviously those associated with him must be if they think

The Budget-Mr. Nowlan they are going to be here next year, but it was suggested in one of the leading financial columns this morning that the minister has established a spread of 5 per cent so that next year he can close the gap entirely and provide other incentives, rather than in income tax as he proposed one year ago. Far be it from me to comment on this degree of optimism at the moment. I will leave that to the Canadian people to decide. I do not think there is any necessity to say anything further on the withholding tax at this time.
I was somewhat disturbed about a matter which is in the minister's budget speech, and to give the background of it I think I should first read a short extract from the speech he made the other night. These words were uttered with all the modesty of the gentlemen opposite who speak on behalf of the government. As found on page 977 of Hansard he said:
Businesses in Canada should make a conscious effort to purchase supplies and components Irom Canadian sources whenever these are competitive-
It sounds to me like good old Tory doctrine, rather than that of a progressive Liberal government. However, the minister no doubt can reconcile that with his conscience.
-to use Canadian professional firms and other services-
I make no comment on that.
-and to carry on in Canada all the industrial functions that can be performed efficiently here, including, particularly, basic industrial research and design.
I must say that I could generally subscribe to that statement but I was somewhat disturbed in reading the budget resolutions dealing with income tax. I do not propose to deal with this in detail because others of my colleagues will, but there is one proposal by the minister in his speech which is, as I said, rather disturbing. It is one dealing with research. I have not had a chance to do all the research work which one would like to do, although "research" perhaps is an improper term at this time. Perhaps I should say all the study which I would like to do.
As I recall the situation, since 1948 the provision in the Income Tax Act dealing with deductions for research has specified that the research work should be done in Canada. I believe this has been the policy of the governments of Canada since that time. At one time this was a matter which caused the government of which I was a member a great deal of concern. Formerly capital deductions could only be made to the extent of 5 per cent. In other words, if you had capital expenditures for research work deductions were allowed only up to 5 per cent of taxable income.

We felt that encouragement should be given to research in Canada and therefore we abrogated the 5 per cent provision and allowed any capital expenditure for research to be deducted from taxable income, provided the research was carried on in Canada. Then we had a problem with respect to encouraging research generally in Canada. We were quite well aware of what was going on. More and more of our scientists and technicians were being attracted south of the border to do research work there. The government of which I had the honour to be a member gave the matter very careful consideration and discussed it with various people in industry, including some who were affiliated with some of those corporations of which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) takes a rather dim view; in other words, subsidiaries of American corporations. We were told by them that we could encourage research work to be done in Canada by giving a bonus and that would result in keeping here some of our students, some of our technicians, some of the men who otherwise would be attracted south of the border. After very careful consideration, of course, the government took the responsibility, or I did-I am not putting the responsibility on any of those with whom we consulted- by saying that we would permit a deduction or an allowance, because it is more than a deduction, of 150 per cent for increased research work which was being done in Canada. We felt this was a proper step to take to encourage technicians, scientists and others engaged in research to remain in Canada since they might otherwise be going to the United States or perhaps abroad. We did this after consultation, as I said, with many corporations that had a very broad experience in these matters.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the proposal which we have in the income tax resolution which will be before us shortly is that the deduction for research may be made when the research is conducted outside of Canada. I think this is a matter to which we should pay special attention.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why don't you issue another writ?

speechtext:
I would suggest that the hon. member must have been listening to CJBC which has been changed to a French language station and he could not understand what was said. I have not been interviewed; I have not spoken to anybody in connection with anything I am saying tonight. If they had the prevision or foresight to deal with this matter, I congratulate them, and I suggest that perhaps my hon. friend will have a very difficult job trying to control them in the city of Toronto in view of the prevision they have shown.
Have we any more questions at this point, Mr. Speaker?
I could go into this subject at greater length, but I know the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) and other hon. members will be dealing with the income tax resolution at greater length. I am simply indicating some of the matters with which we are concerned at the moment. Frankly, this is one of the more fundamental matters. There may be an explanation. I should say that the resolution indicates a retroactive factor going back to 1942. Generally, I know the Minister of Finance would agree with me, retroactive factors should not be included in taxation matters. There may be, and probably is, a very good explanation for it. Possibly there have been some technical flaws in the act heretofore which make it necessary to go back, and I am not quarrelling with that at all. However, I do say one would expect the minister or his parliamentary secretary to give an explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I suggest to him that I think the hon. member means 1962 and not 1942.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If I said 1942, I meant 1962. I know the minister would have obtained more wisdom than he has today if he went back to 1942. He would not have made the mistake he has made. I meant to say 1962. I assume that the minister will give the house an explanation on this matter in due course.
The Budget-Mr. Nowlan
The other matter to which I referred was, why are we departing from the principle that the research work had to be done in Canada in order to qualify for income tax deduction? Perhaps the minister can assure me that I am wrong in this connection. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that both of these questions will be explained fully by the minister when he replies, so I will spend no further time on them.
There is one other matter to which I want to refer, and perhaps I should mention it at this time, although I am not referring to these things in chronological order. The budget, of course, deals with various factors, various features of our economy. I appreciate the fact that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) is here tonight, because I intimated to him that I wanted to raise a matter which I knew would be of interest to him. We are all, of course, concerned with the expanding economy of this country, and our expanding economy generally is determined by our export trade. I must say frankly that I was somewhat disappointed by the answer the Minister of Trade and Commerce gave the other day when I asked him about attendance at the commonwealth conference, which I believe was held yesterday prior to the Geneva conference tomorrow or the next day and for a long time thereafter.
I have no illusions as to the possibility of extending commonwealth trade. I know there are many roadblocks in the way. However, I feel we should pay more attention than ever before to the possibility of at least maintaining, if not developing and extending, our commonwealth trade. I think we were all very proud during the past week, in the light of the reports which we have been receiving concerning the attitude of British troops operating in Cyprus and the way in which they have maintained law and order under great difficulties and great provocation. When we look around us and see the various arguments, such as those in NATO which almost erupted the other day, the problems of the United Nations where, as the Prime Minister said the other night, there can be no solution to our problems if we are going to operate as individual nations, when we think of SEATO and some of the other organizations, we can take some pride in the fact that the commonwealth is a very vital factor in the world organization today.
I think we should give most careful consideration to the maintenance of commonwealth trade relationships and, I know it is difficult, to the extension of them. As I say, I informed the minister I was going to raise
1264	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Nowlan this matter tonight. I think we are all disturbed when we read in the press of a conflict between the European common market on the one hand, the United States and Canada on the other, with the United Kingdom halfway between the two in so far as the importation of agricultural products is concerned. If you read the New York Times, for instance, last Sunday, you would find there was the threat of a conflict between the European common market and the rest of us because they say, as I understand it, there is not going to be any diminution, no accommodation, of tariffs on agricultural products; that is it. "However" they say, "we of course expect you, Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom and other countries to make concessions in negotiations with you in industrial products". On the other hand we read reports in the newspapers in Europe and we see that is not in keeping with the real facts of the case.
Sometimes, Mr. Speaker, I read in the press that there are consultations going on between officials of the Canadian government in Ottawa and officials of the United States government in Washington, and once in a while there are even consultations with the officials of Great Britain. You would think, from reading some newspaper reports, that this was something original, something new, something that had not happened before.
But none of my colleagues in the former government, and I am quite sure also the present Minister of Trade and Commerce, have to be reminded that these conversations and consultations between officials of our two governments are nothing new and nothing original. They have been going on for years, particularly with regard to the possible entry of the United Kingdom into the common market and later with regard to the GATT negotiations, the Kennedy round so-called. As I say they have been going on for two or three years, and the same officials who conducted the negotiations two or three years ago are still conducting them today, and Canada can be very proud of the officials we have representing us.
The only reason I raise this matter at this time and bring it to the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce-although I may have something to say about his estimates in a few moments, to which he might like to listen-is that I would hope during this budget debate he will intervene to bring the House of Commons up to date on a matter which is of vital importance to the economy of the country. I know that he has certain confidences he must maintain and that he cannot disclose all the consultations going on, but within those limitations I hope


he will speak in this debate. That is all I intend to say about the matter at this time.
Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, I am taking longer than I intended to take, but that sometimes happens with an Irishman, even after March 17. The Minister of Finance has referred, not in his budget speech but in the bringing down of the estimates, to the fact that a substantial error was made, apparently by me last year, in dealing with debt costs, interest, management and so on. He made reference to that on two occasions and, even though he did not refer to it in the budget speech, I think I should deal with it now.
It is true that I underestimated the costs of the debt charges when we brought forward the estimates for the year just ended; but that, Mr. Speaker, was not an error in the proper sense of the word. I myself raised this matter with the officials of the Department of Finance when our estimates were being prepared, and I was told it had always been the policy of the Department of Finance, rightly or wrongly, not to accurately estimate the debt charges because obviously, if one did, the experts, the ones with the sharp pencils, the ones who know the intricacies of finance would be able to forecast certain things.
I may interpolate here that the estimates usually come down first and then the budget. The minister, being anxious to get his budget through, brought it down very shortly after the estimates had been tabled this year, but usually there is a time lag of some weeks, and anybody who sees the estimates and studies them, if the carrying charges have been estimated accurately, would be able to estimate what the situation would be during the coming year. Mind you, Mr. Speaker, I could not do it. With all due respect, I doubt if you could; but those in the business, those with the sharp pencils and trained minds would be able to do that.
Therefore not only did I make this error but so did my predecesssors, Hon. Walter Harris, Hon. Douglas Abbott, Right Hon. J. L. Ilsley, Hon. Charles Dunning, Hon. E. N. Rhodes, and Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, going back to the I930's.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What about Hon. J. A.
Robb?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I did not check with regard to Hon. James Robb but my hon. friend opposite, having been in the closet of the privy council throughout those years, will undoubtedly be able to tell me exactly what Hon. James Robb did.
I am not suggesting the Minister of Finance deliberately put an emphasis on this, but

when he referred to it as being an error- in fact he said it was a colossal error on the part of the former minister of finance- I would point out that there were very good precedents for the error which I made, which was in keeping with the policy of the Department of Finance since at least the 1930's.
Also speaking of the estimates perhaps I could interpolate here that apparently the practice is being changed this year. Apparently the minister, after consultation with his officials, decided that the estimates should be made more accurate in anticipation of charges rather than what was the practice heretofore. I have no quarrel with that. It might be, although I am not saying it is, the right practice to follow, but at any rate it will be a departure from the practice of the Department of Finance for the last 30 odd years.
The minister has made provision for education and, of course, as I have said, this was a very prosaic, pedantic budget, and one could understand why; but I would like to point out that within a year or two the minister will be dealing with tremendous demands for the extension of education in Canada. What he has done in this budget is not enough. Just to keep people in high school is not enough. We are going to have to provide facilities, and whether there will be loans to university students or whether there will be fellowships, or whatever there may be, there will have to be provision made for millions of dollars for the extension of our educational facilities.
In this respect I was rather disappointed that there was nothing in the budget which showed any imagination, any preview, any suggestion that we would be confronted with these problems in the future. As a matter of fact these problems are here now, and I rather deplore the fact that this forward looking minister and this government, which had all the answers, completely overlooked that fact in bringing down the budget.
To come now to what is usually considered the root of the budget, that is, the figures, the budgetary deficits, the expenditures and so on and so forth regarding the financial position of the country at this time, the major criticism which could be levelled against this government from this angle is its absolute failure to control the expenditures of the government. If you look at the estimates, pages 4 and 5, Mr. Speaker, you will find more than 50 items of expenditures and over 40 of them show increases over the preceding year.
The increases are very substantial. There are some, of course, which are inevitable. There is, for example, the world fair which
The Budget-Mr. Nowlan is an expenditure that the parliament of Canada has approved, and naturally the government should include that. Then there is the office of the commissioner for representation under our proposed redistribution bill. Obviously there is a substantial expenditure there, and no one can complain about that.
Since the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) is here, perhaps for a moment I could refer to him. I have the figures of various departments but I do not intend to trouble the house with them. However, I should like to refer to this for a moment. You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that last year we created a Department of Industry. Whether there was a divorce or whether some other term might better be used, there was a separation between the old Department of Trade and Commerce and the industrial sector, presumably, so now we have two departments -the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Department of Industry. I think we will all agree, without passing bouquets around at this time, that the Department of Trade and Commerce is one of the more efficiently run departments of the Canadian government. I have no hesitation whatever about saying that. You will remember, too, Mr. Speaker, that we had a Department of Defence Production. This was maintained, as I understand it, in a sort of cold storage but it was to be associated or affiliated with the Department of Industry.
Let us look at the figures for last year. In the main estimates for the year just ending, that is, the year ending on March 31, the Department of Defence Production had $22,700,000-I am dealing, now, with the main estimates, not with the supplementaries. In the coming year, with the creation of the Department of Industry, this figure, the figure for defence production has been reduced to only $17,799,000. But the new Department of Industry has $24,194,000 so that altogether the Department of Defence Production and the Department of Industry have available in the main estimates a total of $41,993,000- perhaps we could call it $42 million-or $19,200,000 more than the Department of Defence Production for last year and the Department of Trade and Commerce which, as I say, is very efficiently run and which has now been divorced of responsibility for industry-it does not have this responsibility at all-and these figures do not include expenditures in connection with the world fair or anything like that, the increase in expenditures for the Department of Trade and Commerce is $9,319,000. That is illustrative of the increase in spending which has taken place in almost every department of the government.
Now let me summarize the main estimates for a moment. The main estimates amount

The Budget-Mr. Nowlan to a total of $6,730 million. The Minister of Finance the other night quite properly estimated that the supplementary estimates might swell the total budgetary expenditure during the coming year to $7,125,000,000-of course, that is an estimate and the hon. gentleman is not committed to it. But this will be the first time our annual budgetary expenditures have gone over the $7 billion mark.
I know there is expansion on all sides. I know that progress demands expansion. I know our population is increasing. I know that old people are living longer, thank heavens, so perhaps I shall live longer, too. I know there are all these expenditures which have to be maintained. But I do think the time has come when the Minister of Finance and the treasury board should pay great attention to the situation which has been reached.
I cannot help wondering what is to happen with regard to the recommendations of the Glassco commission. The minister said in Toronto that various studies were being carried out by industrial research people to consider the recommendations of that commission. A year ago we were told that the recommendations of the commission would be implemented. Now we are told that four industrial research companies are studying the recommendations of the commission and I presume that when they have finished, there will be further industrial research corporations retained to study the findings of these four industrial research corporations. Well, that is not the way to control expenditure in this country.
To understand what is happening, all one needs do is to consider the figures which were given us the other day relative to the advertisements placed by the government in an attempt to secure employment for older men. We were told-and this information was contained in a press release dated March 10 to supplement information given to the house- that 936 people had been placed up to a date early in March, and that we had spent $199,511 on advertisements in connection with their employment. This amounts to the fact that we have spent $213 per man in order to find employment for a few people under this great incentive plan which the Minister of finance indicated as being the answer to our economic problems.
One could go on and on. I have an advertisement here in which I think the Minister of Finance would be tremendously interested. Perhaps the Minister of Trade and Commerce will be interested in it, too. I have an advertisement here for a civil service position. The advertisement is for a morbidity officer. If there is any government which needed a morbidity officer more urgently than the

present one, I have never heard of it. I presume he is to be appointed to the office of Minister of Finance because I cannot imagine anyone who is more morbid than he is.
Mr. Speaker, I promised some of my associates in this house that I would not speak for longer than 20 minutes. I beg their indulgence for having, as an Irishman, so near to March 17, given myself 20 minutes leeway. Having said that, I propose to move, seconded by my hon. friend from Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dins-dale) the following amendment:
That all the words after "that" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
this house regrets that the government has failed to take any effective action to control increasing expenditures and its failure so to do, despite increased taxation imposed at the last session, has resulted in a substantial deficit.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I can understand the difficulty which the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) had in dealing with this budget, because one of the Toronto newspapers which normally supports this government had a somewhat plaintive little headline in it the other day asking whether this Liberal government really could afford quite such a Tory budget. It seemed to me there was a touch of ingratitude in the tones of the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) in his attempts to tear to pieces a budget that should have been right down his alley.
I was interested, too, in the amendment that he proposed. It struck me as a typical example of primitive Tory thinking of which, I may say, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) is not altogether free, either. There seems to be an idea among a great many people-and it is very prevalent in the party to my right-that budgets can be divided into two categories: there are good budgets, and there are bad budgets; and there is a very simple yardstick by which to choose between them-good budgets are those that reduce the deficit; bad budgets are those that increase the deficit. It is a very nice, simple formula; but, of course, it has almost no relevance whatever to a modern, industrial society.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It did not have to them, either.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It did not have to them, either, as my colleague the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) has said. But I think it is as well, perhaps, that we realize this when loud cries are raised against the possibility that we are going to have a deficit, or when our Minister of Finance sticks his chest out and suggests that he is worthy of praise and accolades because he proposes to cut some 33J per cent from the deficit. There may be circumstances in which such a move would be

virtuous, would be wise; there may also be circumstances in which it is supreme tolly, and I suggest that this particular situation is not quite so clearcut as some would have us believe.
This budget, of course, is in very great contrast to last year's. It makes one a little bit nostalgic, perhaps. It really was great fun, of course, when our new Minister of Finance went skipping across the economic fields with all the rest of us and the business world in full cry after him. Then, of course, he stubbed his toe and came to grief. As I say, Mr. Speaker, it was a lot of fun. And events have proved us right; they have proved us to be perfectly right. It was a contradictory budget; he did adopt the wrong methods to achieve the right ends; and finally, of course, it was rather a failure as the chart to the shining new Liberal world that we were to have. But still, Mr. Speaker, I am a little nostalgic, as I say, for that other budget, because even though it was a silly budget; even though it was contradictory; even though it flew in the face of all economic reason, nevertheless it had some qualities that do not attach to the present limp and uninteresting document that we are discussing tonight-because it was an imaginative budget; it was a budget that was designed to accomplish something. The fact that they were foolish methods of accomplishing things does not alter the fact that this was a budget that, shall we say, could be regarded in the modern context; could be regarded as budgets should be regarded today, not merely as the government's housekeeping list but as the government's approach to the whole direction of our economy.
We may have disagreed with what the minister attempted to do, but I do not think any of us could disagree with the aims expressed in that unfortunate budget of last year. The very fact that it was regarded by the minister in a modern context was, I think, very important; and I think it is quite tragic that something has now happened and that, having gained the experience and learned, one would hope, the lesson of how not to accomplish these things, the minister has either chosen or has been unable to follow through with the same type of budget based on sounder principles. It was, of course, regarded, quite rightly, as part of the complex of economic measures by which the government proposed to deal with our complex economy; it was not to be just a housekeeping business.
I think that for a few minutes it might be well if we were to dwell upon what are the real purposes and functions of a budget in this modern age. All too often people seem to think it is merely a casting of accounts. They
The Budget-Mr. Cameron seem to forget that the budget is a complex piece of mechanism which can be used to produce almost any result which those in control of it wish to effect. I suppose one might say its first purpose is that it should be designed to promote an equitable distribution of income, as equitable as is feasible in a fallible world. That, of course, would include dealing with the question of unemployment; dealing with the development of our economy to make sure that all our people have the opportunity to attach themselves to a paying job. It will not do for the Minister of Finance to sweep the unemployed under the rug by labelling them with little figures and saying, "We have an anonymous object in Ontario, which we mark 3 per cent; another anonymous object in British Columbia, which we mark 4 per cent; a much larger anonymous object in Quebec, which we mark 6 per cent; and in the maritimes, where we mark it 8 per cent". These are actual men, women and children, and you cannot push them under the rug and say that because there are fewer of them than there were last year, therefore we do not need to worry very much about them. That, I think, is perhaps one of the first functions of a budget.
Another one, of course, which is connected very closely with it, is the expansion of production in order to effect a wider material base on which to live and build a civilized society. Then I would suggest there is an even more important function of the modern budget and one which is going to become more and more important as time goes on; that is, that it should improve the quality of life for the people of the economy for which it is set up. More and more this is going to become of overriding importance; more and more we are going to find that it is not sufficient merely to arrange that no one is going to starve in our midst, or even to arrange that most people will be living at fairly comfortable levels. Very shortly governments are going to have to assume the responsibility for the very quality of life within the confines of the country. That will entail quite drastic economic measures; not the rather gentle, hesitant ones which we have had to date. It may even entail a complete recasting of our concepts of the purposes of human life.
We are emerging right now from the virtuous Victorian era in which hard work was a virtue no matter what the end of that work might be. We are emerging from the era in which all beauty, shall we say, all the more civilized accompaniments of life had to take second place to the grim business of producing material goods that we could touch and feel and see. It is not going to be good

The Budget-Mr. Cameron enough merely to provide for the material welfare of people. They have to be given the opportunity to live satisfying lives; and they will not live satisfying lives in a barbarous society. Very often when I look on the Canadian scene, it seems to me that we do live in largely a barbarous society in which goals are held before our people that would be appropriate, perhaps, to the savages in Patagonia, perhaps to the native blacks of Australia who have not yet emerged to a higher standard of civilization. But for allegedly civilized people many of the goals that are held before us are trivial, are time wasting and are in fact destructive of the human spirit.
On this question of the equitable distribution of income we have, of course, been moving to some degree in that direction. All our social welfare measures, all our transfer payments, our graduated income tax have been steps toward effecting a more equitable distribution of income. But it has been almost, a snail-like pace at which we have been travelling; and just as snail-like, to my mind, before the fine, clean broom of the Liberal party as it was before the tattered, old besom of the Conservative party. We need to go much faster than we have gone, and there is plenty of room in which to make that progress.
Today I received from a concern in Vancouver, British Columbia, a most interesting little leaflet which to me points to some of the areas in which our Minister of Finance might have moved. I have before me a very tempting advertisement which offers me the opportunity to make tax free capital gains from a very modest investment, tax free capital gains which would be most encouraging, I should think. Certain stocks which one could buy had a low of $6.15 and rose to a high of $21.38, showing an increased book value of 247 per cent. As this advertisement says:
Find the easy way to get that "extra cash" you are looking for.. .tax-free.. .What you make -you keep-all of it.
Then follows a list of stocks which one is advised to buy. Of course, you can lose your shirt, but on the other hand if you do not lose your shirt then, according to this gentleman who has distributed this leaflet, you have great hopes of finally reaching million-airedom. Then there is this pleasant little comment about our modern economy:
Canada is one of the few countries in the world where millions of dollars can be made in the stock market without paying a cent in capital gains taxes. Thousands of traders and speculators from all over have made king-size fortunes here in past years and will continue doing so because of our nation's unlimited wealth in natural resources. We go so far as to suggest that the

profit opportunities will be greater this year than in any previous year in history. Read our financial service for investors, which we mail without charge every week.
One presumes that most of the people who, shall we say, play with this particular outfit will, as I say, lose their shirt.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about Clarkson, Gordon?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, I do not see their names here, and had they been here I might have let the minister know. But presumably there are people who have had more fortunate results from such operations, otherwise these people could not be in business. And they can only be in business because this government, like all its predecessors, Liberal and Conservative, has stubbornly refused to do anything to control capital gains in this country.
We had a striking example of this a few years ago in this chamber when the figures of the capital gains tax-free profits made by those who engaged In the trans-Canada pipe line were revealed. They were almost astronomical sums, and we were informed at that time that not even one five cent piece got into the national treasury. So I suggest that one area in which a more equitable distribution of income could be achieved is by preventing a grossly inequitable distribution of that income, as has taken place so often in the past.
The need for this is plainly evident to anybody who cares to walk through the streets of any of our cities. We do not need any vast tomes of social science analysis; all we need is to walk through some of the streets in the city of Ottawa and then go to some other parts of the city of Ottawa, and we will find a gross disparity of income among Canadians, a disparity that civilized people should be ashamed to maintain. I hope that when the government does come eventually to amend its taxation provisions perhaps it will call on the gentleman whose name I saw mentioned yesterday in the paper, which displayed an extremely attractive photograph and a speculative story that he might be entering the cabinet. I hope he will turn back to the speech he made a year or so ago when he was sitting on the opposition side of the house. I quoted it to him a few months ago and I am not going to quote it again tonight. It is an excellent speech and it will remain an excellent speech; and if, as I hope, and as I am sure all of us hope, this speculation is correct and this gentleman is to be translated to a higher sphere, then he can look forward to having that speech quoted to him quite a number of times, if he does not use the figures he himself

placed upon the record of this house to overcome some of the inequities of our taxation system, thereby improving, as I say, the inequitable distribution of income.
All of us agree that one of the aims of our budgetary provisions-I am speaking in larger terms than merely the housekeeping accounts -should be the expansion of wealth production in the country. This government brought forward a number of measures which were designed to achieve that and also to achieve a wider distribution of wealth producing facilities in the country. The latest reports one hears are that, in spite of the carrots dangled before industry, there have not been too many nibbles and not much anxiety to move into the designated areas, as these days we so politely call the areas not quite so prosperous as other parts of Canada.
I am wondering how long it will be before the government realize that the carrot method is not very efficacious and that something much more drastic has to be done: as drastic, for instance, as was done in Great Britain, not by a forward-looking, progressive Liberal government but by a stale, worn-out Tory government to induce industry to go into areas which they wanted to have developed, by investing large sums of public money in the building of plants and the renting of them to industries who would move in. The Conservative party's weakness, of course, was revealed in the fact that the British taxpayer was forced to subsidize any of these industries which went into such areas, because these industries were given plants at nominal rents. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that before long our government will have to realize that if it is going to overcome the centripetal force that is drawing industry into a few areas of the country they will have deliberately to wrench it away by massive public investment in industry in those undeveloped areas.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that it would be safe to do this, because in spite of the fears of extravagance expressed tonight by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) any of these industries which moved into a designated area are going to be under the control and direction of perhaps the most gimlet-eyed member of the cabinet, and one can hardly imagine too much extravagance being permitted under those gimlet eyes. But I suggest that now is the time that the government must think in those terms. It is not good enough for the Minister of Finance to tell us that because things are economically so cheerful today there is no need to do anything. He rather reminds me of the man who has a leaky roof, and who points out, quite naturally:
The Budget-Mr. Cameron "Of course, I cannot mend the roof when it is raining and there is no need to mend it when it is not raining."
It does not happen to be raining now, but we know quite well that clouds will be coming upon the scene before long and now is the time that our Minister of Finance should get out his little hammer and shingles and get after the roof, while he still has a number of shingles to use, instead of taking pride in having thrown a lot of the shingles away or having failed to obtain the shingles available to him to mend that roof.
I should mention another matter which I thought was, or perhaps should be, one of the purposes of a modern budget, and that is the purpose of improving the quality of life. This to me is really the most serious problem any government faces today. Anyone who observes some of the aspects of the affluent society, both south of the line and our more modest version of it north of the line, must realize all too well the need for vast public investment in what I would call intellectual stimulants badly needed by our people, so that we Canadians do not have, as we so often do, to grimace and shiver at the tastes which our compatriots display in comparison with the tastes displayed by people in more sophisticated areas of the world. But this can only be done by vast expenditures of public funds. Last year I was in Europe and visited a number of quite small cities, much smaller than the city of Ottawa. In fact, they would hardly be called cities in our country. In each case they had a first class symphony orchestra paid for from the revenues of the municipality, and encouraged, I suppose, because almost the whole population turned out to hear the high quality performances they put on. I wondered just what was the difference. Why do these people engage so readily in this sort of expenditure while we shudder away from the very thought of spending even a few dollars on a slight subsidy for a theatrical enterprise or an artistic enterprise of any sort?
I would urge on the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) that it is part of his job to see that the quality of Canadian life is improved in this manner. It will take a vast investment of funds to do so. We hear a great deal about the necessity of expending funds on education, and no one supports this more enthusiastically than I, who had very little opportunity for an education; but it cannot only be formal education. There must be opportunities for people to see the best in art, to hear the best in music. There must be opportunities for people to develop sophisticated and worth-while tastes in the field of literature. Unless we do we are going to

The Budget-Mr. Cameron remain barbarians, and in a world that is rapidly moving we are going to find ourselves in a backwater.
Mention has been made of the drain of scientific brains out of the country, and of the expenditure of public funds by the Canadian authorities on scientific research outside of Canada. Very often we hear complaints made that we spend money on educating young Canadians only to have them leave and go across the border and devote their developed talents to the building up of another economy and another society. I was discussing this matter a month or two ago with a young woman in Vancouver who is an eminent scientist, and she told me that this is quite a wrong picture of the situation, that Canadian scientists have no desire to go to the United States, that it takes more than money to take them there. They are driven there by the fact that there are no employment opportunities for them in Canada. They just cannot find places.
She told me that she herself knew of many young scientists who would have been only too glad to obtain employment in Canada at substantially lower rates than they would receive in the United States, but there were just no places for them. There were no places for them because our Minister of Finance, for one, considers it a virtue to cut down the deficit, considers that he must make obeisances to those rather antiquated gods of orthodoxy when our country is crying out for the type of development that would create substantial employment for such people.
These are things that I think budgets and those who make them should have in mind. The great function of a budget is to improve the quality of life, to increase the quantity of wealth available for supporting that life and also, of course, to fit our country to take part in an effective way in the developmental program that must be undertaken by our United Nations organizations if we are going to have a worth-while world in which a developed Canada can live.
Before closing I should like to say a few words about another matter with which the budget is connected to some degree. Like most Canadians, and certainly, I think, like all intelligent Canadians, I have been disturbed and saddened by the growing rift appearing between two sections of our people, by the increasing bitterness of language, the increasing heat of the exchanges that are being made. I am reminded of something that happened long, long ago, something that I can see across the dark chasm and abyss of time of nearly half a century. I can see quite clearly before my eyes a certain sign that one saw plastered on the walls of every

building in France and Belgium, in estaminets, in cafes, on trains, everywhere where troops were likely to congregate. It was a very simple little sign. Taisez-vous. Mefiez-vous. Les oreilles ennemies vous ecoutent.

Where is the danger? Where are our enemies? Are they in France, in Montreal, in the province of Quebec or elsewhere? No, because we must not look for them without but within ourselves. Our worst enemies are our ears which hear the smallest insults and hurt our pride. They are more dangerous and more insidious than our enemies in France or Montreal.

They are the ears of our malice, of our stupidity, of our ignorance, of our sheer ill will, and those ears are hanging out today to catch every ill considered word, every hurting, wounding comment, every derogatory statement made by one side or the other in this conflict. I feel this very strongly, because unlike most of you here my Canadian national identity was not inherited. It is one I had to build myself bit by bit, and perhaps I built it more strongly or more clearly than at any other time when, as a young man in the uniform of Canada's army, I spent four years in northern Europe.
Significantly enough, a great proportion of those with me at that time were like myself, but there was not one of us there in northern France at that time who was not consciously there as a Canadian representing Canada. We knew, if we had never known before, that Canada was our home, and I suggest that at that time for the first time Canada emerged as a really distinct national identity, and some of us paid a very heavy price for that identity. It is about time we presented our bill and it is a bill which must be paid. That bill is this: We will not permit anyone to destroy that national identity upon which our own identities are based.
The other day when we sent Canadian soldiers to Cyprus the thought occurred to me that perhaps there were some people we might send with that contingent to very good advantage. We might, for instance, pick up the young men who use the term "frog" as an insult, pick up the young men who consider it is the part of patriotism to burn union jacks, and ship them to Cyprus. Take them to Limassol. Take them to Nicosia. Show them the bodies of men, women and children who are dead as the end result of this tossing of insults across the language and cultural fence. I can say from personal experience that there is nothing like a few corpses to induce some serious and salutary thinking in

even the most irresponsible heads on the brevity of human life and the irrevocability of death.
I would hope, Mr. Speaker, that even if we do not send these people from both sides of this country to see the end results of their folly, they may themselves be able to draw a lesson from this. I think most of us felt when the troops went to Cyprus that here was one occasion upon which all of us, whether we be pacifists, militarists or whatever we might be, could be united in our pride in the action being taken by Canada and in the service being performed by Canadians.
In order that we may be able to play a much more effective role in this field in the future, there are those of us who think we should be devoting an even larger part of our substance towards this sort of work. In line with that thought, I wish to present now an amendment to the amendment of the official opposition. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the amendment be amended by deleting therefrom all the words after the words "any effective action", and by substituting therefor the following words:
"reduce defence expenditures so as to provide substantial savings which could be used for economic development in Canada and for increased aid to developing countries through the United Nations and its specialized agencies."
The amendment, as amended, would then read:
This house regrets that the government has failed to take any effective action to reduce defence expenditures so as to provide substantial savings which could be used for economic development in Canada and for increased aid to developing countries through the United Nations and its specialized agencies.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like again to address a plea to those on both sides of this rift that has developed. My plea would be a repetition of that warning that was held before us in France. Taisez-vous, Mefiez-vous. Les oreilles ennemies vous ecou-tent.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In rising to take part in this debate to comment on the contents of the budget, one is faced immediately with the problem of whether he should address his remarks to the contents of the budget or to the omissions from the budget. We in this party acknowledge that there are one or two important proposals in the budget. Having said that, we must hasten to add that there are several matters of even greater importance that received only passing reference. I might say, Mr. Speaker, that paramount amongst these omissions is the enormous increase in the public debt charges. Surely it would be erroneous to assume that
The Budget-Mr. Olson members of the government generally, and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) particularly, are not concerned about the largest of all of the increases in annual public expenditures. If, however, he is concerned and yet did not even mention it in his budget review, then we must assume he does not know what to do about it. Has the minister resigned himself to the belief that this progressively accelerating cost of debt is tantamount to some kind of malignant disease for which there is no treatment or cure? I want to say more about that a little later.
Usually the members of this house, and of course the press, attempt to give a budget a name, a short title that sums up the contents of the budget in a word or two. This practice has been followed again this year. We have heard it called such things as, "stand-by"; a "hold the line budget"; and we have even heard it called the fifth chapter in last year's edition. In addition to that, Mr. Speaker, we see captions in the press referring to this budget as "the students' budget". There is very little substance in it, but the little there is is directed towards giving some assistance to young people. There is the extension of family allowances and the income tax allowance for part-time students. We have no objection to these provisions. I could quote, for example, from our election platform, and also produce a lot of correspondence that has passed between my office and the Department of Finance, to prove that we have advocated the adoption of this measure.
I am wondering whether or not the minister was thinking about the proposal to lower the voting age to 18 years when he prepared the budget. I am sure the minister and the government are very conscious of the fact that by amending the franchise to include the 18-year-olds we would be adding about 750,000 to the voters list. It is obvious this is not a pre-election budget, but perhaps it was a little precultivation which was considered to be prudent. I do not believe the minister had this sole purpose in mind, but when we look at the budget we find everything is the same as last year, except for some of these provisions.
There have been a number of charges levelled since the minister announced he was going to introduce the budget. Some people claimed it was too early; there seemed to be some unnecessary urgency to introduce it. There has even been the suggestion that this may have been done deliberately to harden the attitude of the federal government towards the provincial premiers when they meet in Quebec later this month. I happen to be one of those who believe budgets should
1272	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Olson come out and be introduced before the fiscal year begins with which they deal. Of course, this means they have to be introduced by the middle of March, and that is exactly when the minister introduced it. I am sure we can look back in history and find that the middle of March is the normal time for the introduction of the budget. Sessions of parliament have been thrown out of what might be called the normal pattern during the last two or three years because of elections. When we had the regular four sessions for each parliament, budgets were introduced in March, and I think there is nothing wrong with the timing.
There are one or two comments I should like to make about the minister's statement. I noticed that this year he only made a passing reference to the municipal development and loan board. Last year it was stated this was going to be one of the great new pieces of legislation introduced by the federal government to help the municipalities in Canada with their long term capital requirements problem. I read some of the speeches the minister gave at an earlier time. One of the things he mentioned over and over again when he was talking about the municipal development and loan fund was that it was primarily designed to create employment. I ask, is he satisfied now when we have 5.5 per cent unemployment? Is he satisfied that this and other measures the government introduced have reached their objective to the point where he does not need to extend the activities of the municipal development and loan board?
In his speech the minister referred to:
-the work that will he done, and the new jobs that will be created, as a result of funds made available by the municipal development and loan board
He also referred to the Atlantic development board; but I ask, is the reason that he has not expanded this plan because he is satisfied we have reached the point where there is sufficient employment being created?
At page 971 of his speech, referring to the matter of employment, he said:
This does not mean we can afford to be complacent. Our international deficit has been cut down, but it still remained more than half a billion dollars in 1963. And a level of unemployment around 5 per cent represents only progress-
If the municipal development and loan fund was so successful as he claims it has been, then on his own argument it should be expanded. He says this only represents progress, and that means only the jobs which have been created by the first $400 million, or whatever portion of that which has been spent.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words about regional incentives. The Minister of Finance had quite a lot to say about this


subject. I do not disagree that it is necessary and may have some desirable effects in some areas, but in my opinion having a three year tax holiday in these designated areas, and an accelerated write-off for income tax purposes, will have the effect of some industries being mislocated whenever these incentives are taken away. When that happens employees in an industry that has been improperly located will load a social problem on to the municipality concerned as soon as the incentives are withdrawn.
I should like the minister to take this point into consideration. I know there was one area in southern Alberta which was designated for this purpose. One industry which would have been better established about 120 miles away from that area-

speechtext: The Budget-Mr. Olson Finance, and to put the increase in the 1964-65 fiscal year as compared with the figure for the 1963-64 fiscal year into proper perspective, I want to acknowledge the explanation made to the house by the minister on March 3 when he said that some of this increase was due to inaccurate estimates of the cost for previous years. Surely, one of the most astonishing statements we have heard in this house for years was that made by the former minister of finance this evening, when he told us that ministers of finance for the last 35 years have deliberately deceived parliament and the people of Canada when presenting their estimates in this regard. I want to know whether the present Minister of Finance is following that practice. Is this figure of $1,035 million also intended to mislead the house?

speechtext: I would be glad to answer the question. The answer is no; it is correct.

speechtext:
I am glad we are finally getting some truth. Anyway, regardless of these explanations, the fact remains that the total for the coming year in interest alone stands at $1,005 million. The other $30 million represents amortization of discounts, premiums and commissions and so on. The comparable figure for interest alone for the year ending in 1957 was $508 million. In round figures, this amounts to a $500 million increase in interest charges during the past seven years. I do not think the Minister of Finance will disagree with that figure because it is in the blue books though, once again, I am alarmed to find that these blue books have been deliberately deceiving the house in the past.
This also means there has been an increase of almost 100 per cent during the same seven year period. Let us remember that this is not just a $500 million increase each year, compared with what we paid seven years ago, and every year from now it will go on, unless, of course, we pay off some of it. Projecting the same rate of increase into the future we find that by 1973 the taxpayers of this country will be paying $2 billion in annual debt charges alone.
Moreover, the interest on the debt in the year ending March 31, 1957, amounted to 11.5 per cent of our total expenditure. The interest on debt for the coming fiscal year calls for 15 per cent of the total estimated expenditure. If this pattern continues we shall be devoting 21 per cent of our total estimated expenditure to interest charges by 1973. This increase from 11.5 per cent of the total in 1957 to 15 per cent this year amounts to a 40 per cent rise in the portion of the expenditure incurred by the federal government in debt charges.


These enormous increases, both in themselves and as a percentage of total expenditure, are alarming enough, but even these figures do not tell the whole story. In 1957, current revenue was almost equal to expenditure. This year revenue will be $455 million below expenditure. If one calculates the increased cost of debt in relation to revenue, the percentage of increase appears, therefore, as even greater. This is what is happening, Mr. Speaker. We cannot turn our backs on it. We cannot ignore these charges, because we have to pay them. These debt charges represent by far the largest increase in any item for the year under consideration, yet the minister did not even refer to them in his budget speech.
There are, of course, two very obvious reasons for the tremendous increase which has taken place. The average rate of interest has gone up and the need for loans to meet the deficits of the past six years has added substantially to the principal of our national debt.
I do not have time in which to go into some of these other matters. But we thought we had the minister on the right track just after he brought in his last budget. We understood something was to be done to relieve the tremendous burden of municipal financing. But we do not see any extension of assistance in this regard. According to the latest figures available-and I obtained these figures only a few days ago-municipal debt had increased from $106 million in 1957 to $201 million by 1961. Projecting this rate of increase to 1965 it will be seen that there is likely to be substantially more than a 100 per cent increase during the intervening period. I do not know how much longer the minister thinks this kind of financing can go on, with up to 21 per cent for debt charges alone; municipalities, in some cases, paying 30 per cent to 35 per cent of their total budget for debt interest charges alone. We have heard nothing from the minister to suggest what he is going to do about it or how he is even going to slow down or reverse this trend.
We in the Social Credit party have advocated for years that some of this social capital in the beginning, progressively growing larger, could be subscribed by the Bank of Canada. We know there is an increase in the money supply every year. This year we are told debt charges amount to something like $1,035 million. Is there anything wrong with the Bank of Canada supplying some of the finance and paying it over to the federal treasury so it can be used for these social capital projects? This is all that we ask; we do not ask the government to flood the country with more money, to increase the money supply any faster than it is being increased

now. We think that with regard to some o f these things for which the municipalities incur social capital expenditure it is possible, reasonable and desirable for the Bank of Canada to provide some of the capital. Otherwise we can look into the future-and not too far into the future-to 1973, where the project is that we shall be paying $2 billion in debt charges on the national debt alone. The taxpayers of Canada will also be paying these enormous debt charges through the municipalities. We think the time has come to take the first step, even if it is not a great step, toward reversing this trend.
I think the municipal loan and development fund, if it were changed so that these funds were supplied by the Bank of Canada, would provide that first essential step for us to get back on the rails. I should remind the minister that the New Democratic party are not against deficits. I think if we go back over the years it is rather easy to convince oneself and anyone to whom you are talking that the only time we have had a reasonably high level of prosperity is when somebody has been incurring a deficit. The government, industrial expansion or the expansion of consumer credit, can increase the money supply in the country. But if we are going to have tagging along with it these debts and enormous interest charges that are going to cripple us as the years go by, I think we should be taking a long, hard look at the situation.
We do not ask the government to go all the way and suddenly change things. Perhaps it could be done a little at a time. The money that is required for social capital purposes is called social credit by our party; the New Democratic party call it social capital. This could be taken from the Bank of Canada in stages so we would not have these enormous debt service charges to meet. I see that my time has expired, Mr. Speaker, and I would urge the Minister of Finance to give some consideration to these proposals.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That has been the main theme of the Minister of Finance: the little word "but", after each admission.
What progress did we make with the first budget? We remained at a standstill, we toed the line instead of going ahead.
I realize that after last year's budget, the Minister of Finance might be somewhat afraid. There is a saying: A burnt child shuns the fire. Perhaps that is what happened this year.
At any rate, the last budget is no progress, and where there is no progress, there is a set-back.
Deficits once more. Borrowings once more. A $750 million deficit is predicted. Taxes once more.
What difference is there between the Conservatives and the Liberals? Not the least.
1 am pleased to note that the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) agrees with me. Nothing has changed. At least, the hon. member for Lotbiniere has the courage to admit it and I commend him for it. What difference is there between the budget just introduced and the one submitted by the Conservatives for five or six years? No difference at all. It is always the same. As time goes by, there is more of the same.
There is no use kidding ourselves, nothing has been changed. The Minister of Finance wants us to believe in the economic situation of Canada. Well, Mr. Speaker, I too would like you to believe in the situation which now exists, and I may not see it with the eyes of an accountant or a Minister of Finance, but as we see it in our own offices when we meet electors, workers, farmers, unemployed people of our constituencies who have lost their jobs at the radar station of St. Sylvestre or Parent in the county of Chapleau, or when we talk with unemployed workers from the counties of Lapointe, Villeneuve, or those from the counties of Lake St. John and Lotbiniere.
They know what the situation is in Canada because they have evidence of it in their homes, within their families and all around them. I will try to describe to you the true financial, monetary and economic situation of Canada.
Let us start with the financial situation. The most striking fact about it, Mr. Speaker, is that it is disastrous. The national debt is disastrous, a disaster, that is, for Canada.
To realize that, you just have to refer to the 1963-64 Canada Year Book. Unfortunately, I cannot consult the French edition because I am told it will be published six months after the English edition, because the Minister of Finance is too poor to have the two editions published simultaneously.
Mr. Speaker, our national debt amounted to $17,923 million in 1954. Today, in 1963, it

amounts to $24,799 million, that is an increase of $7 billion. In 1954, the interest amounted to $476 million yearly; in 1963, it amounted to $883 million-pardon me, there is an error of $102 million, as the Minister of Finance pointed out the other day-which brings the interest on the debt to $985 million for 1963 and $1,370 million for 1964.
The interest is disastrous and so is the debt. Mr. Speaker, the government keeps on borrowing and the Minister of Finance has announced that he will seek to borrow $750 million this year.
That is the debt of the federal government. There are also the debts of the provincial governments, the school boards, the municipalities. In 1960-the last year for which a complete report is available-the debt of the federal government amounted to $21,369 million, the provincial debts amounted to $3,699 million and the municipal debts to $4,771 million, that is a total of $29,565 million.
A debt of $30 billion for the government, whereas the money in circulation to cover that amount is barely $2,500 million, plus the money in cheques; the money supply totals between $16 and $17 billion, probably even a little less, perhaps $15 or $16 billion this year, which means that there is not enough money in circulation to pay the whole debt.
The federal government debt alone amounts to $8 billion more than all the money Canadians have in hand, in their bank accounts, in companies' chests, in savings of all kinds and everywhere in Canada.
What is to be done when one has more debts than assets?
Mr. Speaker, I wish to put a question to the Minister of Finance. I am sure that, as an accountant, he will be able to give me an answer. I am told that his parliamentary secretary (Mr. Benson) is also an accountant. Here is my question. How do you call a company or corporation whose debts are greater than its assets? Do not be shy about telling us. It is a bankrupt company. Well, the federal government alone has a debt exceeding by $8 billion its assets in cash, cheques, legal tender, money supply or credit in circulation.
But notice, Mr. Speaker, that the federal government likes to be in debt. It likes to borrow. I wonder if it is still qualified to administer the country.
I was reading today what the functions of the government are with regard to boards and corporations and I found the information appalling.
It likes to borrow, and the best solution it has to offer Canadians is to get deeper

into debt. And you will realize it by the examples I shall provide.
First of all, there is the municipal loans board. Let us loan to the municipalities, this will help them.
We shall establish a commission to help students. We shall lend them money; we shall help them to run into debt.
There are also the loans to farmers through the Farm Credit Corporation, and under the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act. Let us lend to farmers, let us involve them in debt. This will please my friend, the hon. member for Lotbiniere. Let us involve them in debt.
There is also the industrial development bank. Let us lend to manufacturers.
And the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, on the other hand, lends to Canadian taxpayers, so that they may be able to build houses.
Such is the federal government. It likes to lend. It likes to get everybody into debt.
There are also the loans for farm improvements. Again, let us get our farmers into debt.
And as concerns immigrants to Canada, let us lend them money, let us get them into debt, also and this, according to the Revised Statutes of Canada, chapter 325, section 69, paragraph (6).
And it was also necessary to lend to Indians. An Indian loans board was established, according to chapter 149, section 69, paragraph (6) of the revised statutes. Let us involve them in debt.
There are also loans to the international development association, 1960 statutes, chapter 32, section 5.
And what about loans to crown corporations? It is not enough to get everybody into debt, loans are also intended for crown corporations. The government sets up crown corporations and lends them money under Revised Statutes of Canada, chapter 116, section 82, paragraph 4.
We have the small business loans. We even have loans for fishing operations. Briefly, everybody is being put into debt.
Mr. Speaker, I only quoted a few of the loans acts. And when everybody has been involved into debt, regulations are passed to control credit arrangements for the Canadian people.
Once all the taxpayers are well into debt, regulations are passed to assist the creditors.
Business of the House
Reference is made in our statutes to the Bankruptcy Act regulations.
We have regulations on arrangements between creditors and farmers, Revised Statutes of Canada, chapter 111, section 41, paragraph 2.
There is also a statute providing for the adjustment of debts contracted for seed grain loans.
Mr. Speaker, it means that the function of government has changed. It is no longer an administrator or a legislator. It does not exist any more to see to the welfare of the citizens, but rather to lend them money, to get them into debt. Loans are made to everybody.
Does the government suggest solutions or logical measures to help the Canadian people? No. It makes loans to them, it gets them into debt.

subtopic: REPORT BY A JOINT COMMITTEE ON COMMUNITY ANTENNA TELEVISION BY THE BOARD OF BROADCAST GOVERNORS AND THE DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT TO THE HONOURABLE J. W. PICKERSGILL, MINISTER OF TRANSPORT AND TO THE HONOURABLE MAURICE LAMONTAGNE, SECRETARY OF STATE

speechtext:
On December 31, 1963, the Secretary of State and the Minister of Transport issued a public statement in which they said that the board of broadcast governors-with the technical advice and in consultation with the Department of Transport-had been asked by the government to inquire into and recommend any legislative action that may be required to ensure that, so far as the constitutional jurisdiction of parliament will permit, the use of community antenna television for the dissemination of television programs is subject to similar regulation under parallel conditions to that applied to direct broadcasting.
A committee of the board of broadcast governors and the Department of Transport- and under it a working subcommittee of the same two agencies-has inquired into this subject over the past two months and has held numerous discussions and formal meetings.
Community antenna systems rely both upon radio links and land lines or cable relays. Complete control of all aspects of cable relays and closed circuit T.V. can be achieved only by complete federal control of land lines, a large portion of which are presently under provincial control in the absence of federal declaration or statute. This would involve complicated problems of provincial consultation. However, effective control over the major area of CATV could be achieved by amendments to the Broadcasting Act covering commercial broadcasting receiving stations and land stations where these stations are used to feed a cable relay distribution system with radio or television broadcasting signals or where the land stations are used to feed the distribution systems with closed circuit radio or television signals. These amendments should include:
(1)	a requirement that the Minister of Transport refer to the B.B.G. for hearing and recommendation of any applications for licences or for renewal thereof, including renewal of existing licences, and give the board the necessary powers for this purpose;
(2)	authority for the board to regulate such stations in regard to program content and
other non-technical matters (the Department of Transport would continue to deal with technical aspects);
(3)	extension of the objects and purposes of the act to commercial broadcasting receiving stations and to land stations feeding cable relay distribution systems;
(4)	a limit on foreign ownership of new commercial broadcasting receiving stations and land stations feeding cable relay systems similar to the limitations now contained in the act for broadcasting stations;
(5)	authority for the board to control interconnections (networks) of cable relay distribution systems when they are fed with signals from commercial broadcasting receiving stations or land stations.
(6)	authority for the board to enforce of its own action conditions of licences of stations in these categories where the conditions have been included as a result of a recommendation from the board; and to take action in the courts of violations of such conditions or of infractions of the regulations.
When authority is given to the board under the act, it is proposed the board should regulate the commercial broadcasting receiving stations and the land stations as defined in such a manner to ensure that, consistent with the public interest in the reception of a varied and comprehensive broadcasting service, the board should to the greatest extent practicable maintain the Canadian identity and character of service available to the public and further the purposes of broadcasting as set out in section 10 of the act. The board would also regulate the relationship between licencees and provide for the final determination of all matters and questions in relation thereto.
The board may wish to consider regulations prescribing the time periods for programs delivered by commercial broadcasting receiving stations and land stations as defined for feeding a cable relay system, and respecting the alteration or curtailment of programs handled by these two sources for feeding a cable relay system. Changes in the authority for the reception of broadcasting stations by

commercial broadcasting receiving stations and the broadcasting signals carried by land stations as defined would need to come to the board for approval, as would a change in the area served through the medium of the cable relay system as specified in the licence.
The committee has examined the act in detail and is prepared to lend its assistance to the Department of Justice in suggesting the necessary changes and wording in the Broadcasting Act to cover cable relay systems.
Friday, March 20, 1964
